choices.r: Tempting if you choose the test from the table's layout, seeing the three age groups as separate groups to compare — but homogeneity requires a separate random sample (or randomly assigned treatment group) for each group, and here one sample of 300 was classified two ways. Fix: ask 'how many samples were taken?' and, when it is one sample measured on two variables, choose independence.
choices.t: A test of homogeneity, because the table compares news source across the three age groups.

choices.r: Tempting if you see 'compare groups' and reach for the two-sample test for proportions you already know — but that test compares two groups on a yes/no outcome, and here there are three age groups and three news sources. Fix: count the rows and columns of the table, and if either is more than two, use a chi-square test.
choices.t: A two-sample z-test for proportions, because age groups are being compared.

choices.r: This earns the point because homogeneity versus independence depends on the study design. One sample, cross-classified by two variables, calls for independence.
choices.t: A test of independence, because one random sample was classified on two categorical variables.

choices.r: Tempting if you rely on a memorized shortcut such as 'three rows means homogeneity' — but the choice between homogeneity and independence depends on how the data were collected, not on the number of rows. Fix: decide from the sampling design: separate samples per group means homogeneity, one sample with two variables means independence.
choices.t: A test of homogeneity, because chi-square tests with three rows always test whether distributions are the same.

stem: A researcher randomly selects 300 adults from one city and records each person's age group (18–34, 35–54, 55 and over) and preferred news source (TV, online, print). The counts are displayed in a table. Which chi-square test applies, and why?
subject: ap-statistics

choices.r: Tempting if you flip the condition and read the p-value as the probability that H₀ is true given the data — but the p-value is computed by assuming H₀ is true, so it cannot be the probability that H₀ is true. Fix: begin every p-value interpretation with 'Assuming H₀ is true,' and then describe the chance of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
choices.t: There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis H₀ is true, given the sample result.

choices.r: Tempting if you subtract the p-value from 1 and read 0.97 as the probability that Hₐ is true — but a p-value gives no probability for either hypothesis. Fix: do not subtract the p-value from 1; interpret 0.03 directly as the chance of a result this extreme if H₀ is true.
choices.t: There is a 97% chance that the alternative hypothesis Hₐ is true, given the sample result.

choices.r: This earns the point because a p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true and measures how unusual the sample result is under that assumption.
choices.t: If the true proportion were 0.30, there would be a 3% chance of getting a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed.

choices.r: Tempting if you read 0.03 on the same scale as the proportion 0.30 and treat it as the gap between the sample proportion and 0.30 — but the p-value is a probability, not a difference in proportions. Fix: when you see a p-value, ask 'the probability of what?' and answer with the chance of a sample proportion at least as large as the observed one under H₀.
choices.t: The sample proportion is 3 percentage points above the hypothesized value of 0.30.

stem: A significance test of H₀: p = 0.30 versus Hₐ: p > 0.30 produces a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation of the p-value is correct?
subject: ap-statistics

This would make the SE smaller than 2.

stem: What sample size is needed?
stimulus: A researcher wants SE = 2 when σ = 10.
subject: ap-statistics

choices.t: 0.20; it is the exact probability, because 100 trials were used.

choices.t: 0.16; it is an estimate that would change in a new simulation, and more trials would make it more reliable.

choices.r: Correct: (16 + 4)/100 = 0.20; a simulation gives an estimate that changes from run to run and becomes more reliable with more trials.
choices.t: 0.20; it is an estimate that would change in a new simulation, and more trials would make it more reliable.

choices.t: 0.20; it is an estimate, and fewer trials would make it more reliable.

stem:
A student simulates flipping a fair coin 5 times and records the number of heads, repeating this for 100 trials.
Heads = 0: 3 trials
Heads = 1: 15 trials
Heads = 2: 32 trials
Heads = 3: 30 trials
Heads = 4: 16 trials
Heads = 5: 4 trials
Based on this simulation, what is the estimated probability of at least 4 heads, and which statement about it is best?
subject: ap-statistics

choices.t: The claim is not supported; the interval suggests group B has the higher proportion, since every plausible value of p_B - p_A is positive.

stem: A 95% confidence interval for p_B - p_A, the difference in the proportions of all voters who support a candidate in group B and in group A, is (0.04, 0.12). A pollster claims that group A has the higher proportion. Which statement is correct?
subject: ap-statistics

choices.t: Approximately normal with mean 0.15 and standard deviation 0.00245.

stem: Among all users of app A, 40% renew their subscription, and among all users of app B, 25% renew. Independent random samples of 200 users of app A and 150 users of app B are selected, and the difference in sample proportions (p-hat A - p-hat B) is recorded. Which statement describes its sampling distribution?
subject: ap-statistics

choices.t: When x = 0, y increases by 0.8.

stem: What is the best interpretation of the slope?

subject: ap-statistics

choices.r: Tempting if you count 7 'make' digits and forget that skipping 0 leaves only 9 equally likely digits — so a make gets probability 7/9, about 78%, not 70%. Fix: compute (number of make digits) / (number of digits in use) and check that it equals 0.70.
choices.t: Let digits 1 to 7 be a made shot and 8 and 9 a miss, skipping 0; one trial is four digits.

choices.r: Tempting if you mix up one shot with one trial and simulate the shots one digit at a time — but the event 'at least 3 of 4 made' needs four shots per trial, and the percent of made shots estimates 0.70, not the target probability. Fix: define one trial as one full run of the process (four shots) and record whether the event happened in that trial.
choices.t: Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot and 7 to 9 a miss; one trial is a single digit; record the percent of made shots.

choices.r: This earns the point because 7 of 10 digits give a 70% chance per shot, one trial models the four shots, and the recorded result is the event of interest. Many repeated trials let the relative frequency approach the true probability.
choices.t: Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot and 7 to 9 a miss; one trial is four digits; record whether at least three are made; repeat for many trials.

choices.r: Tempting if you confuse the four shots within a trial with the number of trials to run — but with only four trials the estimate can only be 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1 and swings widely from run to run. Fix: run many trials (for example, 100 or more) so the relative frequency settles near the true probability.
choices.t: Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot, use four digits, but run only four trials and report that proportion.

stem: A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. A student wants to estimate by simulation the probability that she makes at least 3 of her next 4 free throws, using a random digit table with digits 0 to 9. Which design is valid?
subject: ap-statistics

choices.r: That is the probability of a single success, not zero successes in five trials.
This is not the correct binomial calculation for zero successes.
That is the trial count, not a probability.

stem: What is P(X = 0)?
stimulus: A binomial setting has n = 5 and p = 0.5.
subject: ap-statistics

choices.r: G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have two, so this reverses the numbers.
choices.t: Primer 1's duplex, because A-T pairs have more hydrogen bonds than G-C pairs.

choices.r: Equal length does not mean equal stability when the base composition differs.
choices.t: Both duplexes separate at the same temperature, because both are 20 base pairs long.

choices.r: Base pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds, and A-T pairs are weaker.
choices.t: Primer 1's duplex, because it has more A-T pairs and A-T pairs are covalent bonds.

choices.r: Correct: Primer 1 has 8 x 3 + 12 x 2 = 48 hydrogen bonds and primer 2 has 14 x 3 + 6 x 2 = 54, so primer 2 duplex needs more energy to separate.
choices.t: Primer 2's duplex, because it has 14 G-C pairs, giving 54 hydrogen bonds compared with 48 for primer 1.

stem: Two 20-nucleotide primers are designed to bind a target DNA strand. Primer 1 has 8 G-C pairs when bound, and primer 2 has 14 G-C pairs when bound. The remaining pairs are A-T. Which statement best predicts which duplex requires a higher temperature to separate and why?
subject: biology

choices.r: Nucleic acid type confusion: substituting RNA changes the sugar and replaces thymine with uracil without removing complementarity. Complementary RNA therefore does not isolate the effect of nucleotide order. Fix: Compare the replacement’s base pairing and sugar type before selecting the control.
choices.t: Replace the second sheet’s strands with complementary RNA strands containing uracil instead of thymine.

choices.r: Amount-versus-sequence confusion: increasing strand number tests availability, not complementary order. The added strands still have the matching sequence, so this comparison cannot isolate whether matching is required. Fix: Identify which property changes, and confirm it is sequence complementarity rather than strand amount.
choices.t: Place twice as many of the original complementary DNA strands on the second sheet.

choices.r: Missing-component baseline trap: removing all partner strands eliminates both their presence and their complementarity. Reduced pairing would not distinguish a requirement for matching order from a requirement for any partner strand. Fix: Keep partner strands present while changing only their ability to match the connectors.
choices.t: Use a second sheet with no nucleic acid strands attached.

choices.r: This comparison preserves strand length, base composition, and DNA identity while changing sequence complementarity. A decrease in pairing would support the importance of matching A–T and C–G bases along the strands, rather than simply having those bases present.
choices.t: Replace the second sheet’s strands with DNA strands of equal length and identical base counts, arranged in a noncomplementary sequence.

stem: A materials laboratory uses DNA strands to fasten two thin sheets together. One sheet carries 18-nucleotide single-stranded DNA connectors; the other carries antiparallel, complementary DNA strands. Researchers measure the percentage of connectors paired with strands on the second sheet. They want to determine whether pairing requires complementary nucleotide order rather than merely the same collection of bases. Which comparison treatment best isolates this variable? Apart from the stated change, strand amounts and experimental conditions remain constant.
subject: biology

choices.r: Label reaches the Golgi complex and leaves the cell at the normal times, so ER-to-Golgi transport is not blocked.
choices.t: Vesicle transport from the rough ER to the Golgi complex is blocked in the mutant cells.

choices.r: Insulin is released at the normal time, so exocytosis works.
choices.t: Exocytosis is blocked, so insulin builds up in vesicles inside the mutant cells.

choices.r: The timing of label entering the rough ER is normal, so synthesis speed does not explain the missing modifications.
choices.t: Ribosomes in the mutant cells make the protein too slowly, so it cannot be modified.

choices.r: Correct: Label reaches every compartment and leaves the cell on schedule, so trafficking is intact; the released protein is chemically unmodified, which points to defective modifying enzymes.
choices.t: Transport between compartments works, but the enzymes that modify the protein as it moves through the ER and Golgi complex are defective.

stem: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin. In mutant cells, the timing of radioactive label is the same as in normal cells: rough ER at 2 minutes, Golgi complex at 15 minutes, secretory vesicles at 30 minutes, and outside the cell at 60 minutes. However, the insulin released by mutant cells lacks the carbohydrate and other chemical changes that normal insulin has. Which statement best explains the results?
subject: biology

choices.r: Reversed packing effect: This prediction treats double bonds as promoting tighter packing. Their kinks instead reduce close packing, so increased unsaturation favors a more liquid state at the same temperature. Fix: Trace double bonds → kinks → reduced packing before predicting physical state.
choices.t: The stored fats will tend to be less liquid while continuing to serve as a long-term energy reserve.

choices.r: Liquid–soluble confusion: A more liquid state does not mean greater water solubility. Increasing unsaturation does not make fats hydrophilic or remove their energy-storage function. Fix: Evaluate physical state and water solubility separately.
choices.t: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid and become water-soluble, preventing them from serving as an energy reserve.

choices.r: Lipid-class interchangeability: This prediction assigns the membrane-forming role of phospholipids to fats. Altering fatty acid unsaturation does not convert stored fats into phospholipids. Fix: Identify the lipid class before assigning its biological function.
choices.t: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid and form phospholipid bilayers instead of serving as an energy reserve.

choices.r: Unsaturated fatty acids contain carbon–carbon double bonds that introduce kinks, reducing close packing and favoring a more liquid state. Changing the degree of unsaturation does not eliminate the energy-storage function of fats.
choices.t: The stored fats will tend to be more liquid while continuing to serve as a long-term energy reserve.

stem: A change in a mammal’s diet increases the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in its stored fats. The total mass of stored fat and the lengths of the fatty acid chains remain unchanged. At the same temperature, which prediction best connects the structural change to the properties and function of the stored fats?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct. Distilled water is hypotonic to the celery cells, so water enters by osmosis. The cell wall resists expansion, generating turgor pressure that makes the tissue rigid and prevents the plasma membrane from rupturing.
choices.t: The cellulose cell wall resists expansion after water enters, so rising turgor pressure limits further swelling and prevents lysis.

choices.r: Incorrect. Water crosses plant cell membranes by osmosis, often through aquaporins. Rigidity results from water entry and turgor pressure, not from blocking water movement.
choices.t: The plant plasma membrane becomes impermeable to water in distilled water, so the cell wall remains rigid because no osmosis occurs.

choices.r: Incorrect. Net water movement stops when rising turgor pressure counteracts the osmotic gradient, not when the cytoplasm becomes isotonic with distilled water -- true isotonicity with distilled water is never reached in an intact walled cell.
choices.t: Water enters until the cytoplasm becomes isotonic with the surrounding water, at which point net movement stops and the cell stays intact.

choices.r: Incorrect. Distilled water is hypotonic relative to both plant and animal cell cytoplasm. The key difference is that plant cells have a rigid wall that develops turgor pressure; animal cells lack that wall and may lyse.
choices.t: Plant cells avoid lysis because their cytoplasm is always isotonic to distilled water, while animal cells are hypertonic to distilled water.

stem: Which best explains why celery in distilled water becomes rigid rather than lysing, unlike animal cells in hypotonic solution?
stimulus: A student places strips of celery into three solutions for 30 minutes: (1) distilled water, (2) dilute salt solution, and (3) concentrated salt solution. After 30 minutes, the strip in distilled water is rigid and crisp; the strip in dilute salt solution is slightly flexible; the strip in concentrated salt solution is limp and wilted. The student notes that unlike red blood cells placed in distilled water, the celery does not burst.
subject: biology

choices.r: Heads are polar and would avoid hexane, and tails would not surround water.
choices.t: Phosphate heads face the hexane and tails surround the water droplet.

choices.r: Correct: In a nonpolar solvent the polar heads cluster around the water and the tails extend into the hexane, the reverse of the arrangement in water.
choices.t: Phosphate heads face the water droplet in the center and fatty acid tails extend into the hexane.

choices.r: A bilayer with water on both sides forms in water, but here the surrounding liquid is hexane.
choices.t: Phospholipids form a double layer with water on both sides of it.

choices.r: The interactions are hydrogen bonds between heads and water and hydrophobic effects, not covalent bonds between tails and water.
choices.t: Phospholipids join the water droplet by covalent bonds between the tails and the water molecules.

stem: Phospholipids are dissolved in a nonpolar liquid, hexane, and a few drops of water are added. Small spherical structures form, each trapping a tiny water droplet. Which arrangement best explains the structures?
subject: biology

choices.t: Sample 1, because it contains only one type of monomer.

choices.r: Correct: Samples 1 to 3 break down into many repeating monomers (monosaccharides, amino acids, nucleotides), but a triglyceride is built from one glycerol and three fatty acids.
choices.t: Sample 4, because it is assembled from glycerol and three fatty acids rather than a chain of repeating monomers.

choices.r: Proteins are polymers even though they contain about 20 types of amino acid monomers.
choices.t: Sample 2, because it contains more than one kind of monomer.

choices.r: Each nucleotide has three parts, but nucleic acids are chains of many nucleotide monomers and are polymers.
choices.t: Sample 3, because its products contain three different parts.

stem: Four purified samples are completely hydrolyzed and the products are identified. Sample 1 gives only one kind of six-carbon sugar, with many molecules per original molecule. Sample 2 gives many molecules from about 20 kinds of compounds that each have an amino group and a carboxyl group. Sample 3 gives four kinds of compounds, each with a nitrogenous base, a sugar, and phosphate. Sample 4 gives, per original molecule, one three-carbon alcohol and three long-chain fatty acids. Which sample is NOT a polymer made of a long chain of repeating monomers, even though it was assembled by dehydration synthesis?
subject: biology

choices.t: The cytoplasm of S-phase and M-phase cells contains diffusible regulators that can push a nucleus from G1 into that phase.

choices.r: A G1 nucleus with unreplicated DNA began to replicate and to condense after fusion, so DNA amount alone does not set the stage.
choices.t: The stage of a cell is set only by the amount of DNA in its nucleus, with no role for cytoplasmic factors.

choices.r: The factors acted across the fused cytoplasm, so they were able to move from one nucleus to another.
choices.t: Regulators of the cell cycle stay inside the nucleus and cannot move between cells.

choices.r: The G1 nucleus responded to the signals from the partner cell, so it was not blocking S and M phase.
choices.t: G1 nuclei hold inhibitors that stop S and M phase from starting.

stem: In a classic experiment, researchers fused cells at different stages of the cell cycle. When a G1 cell was fused to a cell in S phase, the G1 nucleus began to replicate DNA early. When a G1 cell was fused to a cell in M phase, the G1 nucleus condensed its chromosomes. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Water molecules keep their partial charges while hydrogen bonding, and conductivity depends on free ions, not on water losing charge.
choices.t: Sugar dissolves by forming bonds with water that remove all charge from the water molecules.

choices.r: Dissolving sugar does not break covalent bonds within the sugar molecule, so atoms are not released.
choices.t: Sugar dissolves because water breaks its covalent bonds into individual atoms, which carry no charge.

choices.r: Sugar has many polar -OH groups and is not nonpolar, and a nonpolar substance would not dissolve well in water.
choices.t: Sugar is nonpolar, so it dissolves by being trapped between water molecules without any attraction to them.

choices.r: Correct: Conduction requires free ions; sugar's polar -OH groups hydrogen bond with water so the molecules disperse intact without becoming ions.
choices.t: Sugar stays as intact, uncharged molecules whose many -OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so no free ions are produced.

stem: Two clear solutions are prepared by dissolving 10 g of table salt (NaCl) in one beaker of water and 10 g of sugar (C12H22O11) in another. A conductivity probe shows that the salt solution conducts electricity well and the sugar solution does not conduct. Both solids dissolve completely. Which statement best explains why the sugar solution does not conduct even though the sugar dissolved?
subject: biology

choices.r: Early pre-biotic systems did not require the metabolic throughput of modern cells. Slow catalysis is consistent with viability in a pre-cellular context. The existence of self-replicating ribozymes directly refutes the claim that RNA cannot catalyze.
choices.t: RNA cannot have been the original catalyst because its kcat is too low to sustain any metabolism

choices.r: Ribosomal proteins are structural scaffolding, not catalytic. The RNA core performs peptide bond formation. Concluding proteins came first based on the ribosome inverts the actual evidence.
choices.t: Proteins must have preceded RNA because the ribosome requires protein subunits to function

choices.r: Mg²⁺ is a cofactor that enhances RNA catalysis, not a replacement catalyst. The evidence positions RNA as the primary catalyst, with metal ions as assistants — not the other way around.
choices.t: Mg²⁺ ions were the original catalysts in pre-biotic chemistry; RNA evolved later to replace metal-ion catalysis

choices.r: Ribozymes can self-replicate (information + catalysis combined), and RNA's catalytic role in translation (the ribosome) was conserved even after protein enzymes evolved. Proteins superseded RNA catalytically because they are far faster, while Mg²⁺-assisted RNA catalysis was sufficient in pre-biotic conditions.
choices.t: RNA likely served as both the informational and catalytic molecule before proteins; proteins later took over most catalysis because they are faster, while RNA's catalytic role in translation was retained

stem: Which conclusion about early life is best supported by integrating all three pieces of evidence?
stimulus: Evidence supporting the RNA World hypothesis includes: (1) ribozymes that catalyze their own replication in vitro; (2) the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center — which forms peptide bonds — is composed entirely of RNA; ribosomal proteins are structural, not catalytic; (3) a self-replicating ribozyme catalyzes its reaction roughly 10,000× more slowly than a typical protein enzyme, and its rate increases about 50-fold when Mg²⁺ is added.
subject: biology

choices.r: Experiment 2 shows the enhancer must be paired with a promoter (the luciferase reporter's promoter) to drive expression — the enhancer alone is not sufficient and does not contain an independent promoter. Enhancers work by looping to contact and activate proximal promoters, not by independently initiating transcription.
choices.t: The enhancer contains its own promoter that independently drives Gene X transcription; the Gene X promoter is dispensable

choices.r: Each experiment supports a distinct, narrower conclusion: (1) deletion in liver cells drops expression to near zero -- the enhancer is necessary; (2) the enhancer drives strong reporter expression in liver cells -- it is transcriptionally active there; (3) the same construct is inactive in muscle cells -- its activity is cell-type-restricted; (4) adding liver-specific transcription factors to muscle cells restores activity -- the enhancer's activity depends on those factors, and supplying them is sufficient to rescue it in a cell type where it was otherwise silent.
choices.t: The enhancer is necessary for Gene X transcription in liver cells, drives strong expression when linked to a reporter gene in liver cells, and requires liver-specific transcription factors -- supplying those factors to muscle cells restores the enhancer's activity there

choices.r: Experiment 1 (deletion in adult liver cells drops expression to near zero) directly contradicts this hypothesis. If Gene X maintained itself independently after initial activation, deleting the enhancer in already-expressing liver cells would have no effect. The enhancer is continuously required for maintained expression.
choices.t: The enhancer is required only for the initial activation of Gene X during liver development; once activated, Gene X maintains its own expression through a positive feedback loop independent of the enhancer

choices.r: Experiment 3 shows the enhancer-reporter construct is inactive in muscle cells — but this is most simply explained by the absence of liver-specific activating transcription factors (as confirmed by experiment 4). There is no evidence from these experiments that the enhancer recruits muscle-specific repressors; absence of activators in muscle is sufficient to explain the muscle-specific silence.
choices.t: The enhancer acts as a silencer in muscle cells by actively recruiting repressor proteins that block Gene X transcription in non-hepatic tissues

stem: Which conclusion about the liver-specific enhancer is best supported by the experimental results?
stimulus:
A gene (Gene X) is expressed at high levels in liver cells but not in muscle cells. The same DNA sequence (same gene) is present in both cell types. Researchers identify a 300 bp enhancer element located 50 kb upstream of Gene X's promoter. Experiments:

1. Deleting the enhancer in liver cells: Gene X expression drops to near zero.
2. Inserting the 300 bp enhancer upstream of a reporter gene (luciferase) in liver cells: luciferase is strongly expressed.
3. Inserting the same enhancer-luciferase construct into muscle cells: luciferase is not expressed.
4. Adding liver-specific transcription factors to muscle cells (via transfection) with the enhancer-luciferase construct: luciferase is expressed.
subject: biology

choices.r: Length–sequence confusion: Equal numbers of amino acids do not establish identical sequences. The different amino acid at position 72 changes primary structure even though chain length stays constant. Fix: Check amino acid identity and order when comparing primary structures.
choices.t: The forms have the same primary structure because both contain 180 amino acids, so their different performance cannot involve an amino acid sequence difference.

choices.r: The supported force drops from 8 N to 3 N alongside a change in folded shape. Changing an amino acid’s R group can alter folding interactions, linking the sequence difference to a shape change and reduced structural support.
choices.t: The replacement form is less compact and supports less force, consistent with altered R-group interactions changing folding and structural support.

choices.r: Side-chain–backbone confusion: A difference in R groups is not a break in the peptide backbone. The stem specifies unbroken chains of equal length, ruling out shortening as the explanation. Fix: Distinguish altered side-chain interactions from broken bonds connecting amino acids.
choices.t: The replacement form supports less force because the R-group change breaks backbone peptide bonds, producing a shorter protein.

choices.r: Tertiary–quaternary confusion: Overall folding within one polypeptide concerns tertiary structure. Quaternary structure describes associations between multiple polypeptides, whereas each protein molecule here contains only one. Fix: Identify how many polypeptides form each protein before naming its structural level.
choices.t: The replacement form supports less force because its less compact folding indicates a change in quaternary structure.

stem:
A materials laboratory tests two forms of a structural protein that helps a soft gel withstand compression. Every protein molecule contains a single, unbroken polypeptide of 180 amino acids. The forms differ only at amino acid position 72. Gels containing equal amounts of either form are tested under the same conditions.

Protein form | R group at position 72 | Overall folded shape | Maximum force supported before gel collapses (N)
Standard | Charged | Compact | 8
Replacement | Uncharged and hydrophilic | Less compact | 3

Which interpretation connects the measured relationship to protein structure and function?
subject: biology

choices.r: Bond-integrity trap: Keeping peptide-bond connectivity unchanged does not preserve the amino acid sequence when an amino acid is replaced. The altered sequence can change folding and function. Fix: Compare the original and replacement amino acid identities before judging whether primary structure changed.
choices.t: Unchanged peptide-bond connectivity preserves primary structure, so the protein must retain its original shape recovery.

choices.r: Secondary–tertiary confusion: Secondary structure involves hydrogen bonding between backbone atoms, not ionic interactions between R groups. The disrupted R-group interaction instead contributes to tertiary folding. Fix: Locate each interaction on the backbone or R groups before assigning a structural level.
choices.t: The replacement directly changes secondary structure, which is defined by ionic interactions between R groups, impairing shape recovery.

choices.r: The nonpolar R group cannot maintain the original ionic interaction with the remaining charged R group. Losing this stabilizing interaction may change the protein’s three-dimensional shape and impair the shape recovery required for its mechanical function.
choices.t: Loss of the ionic interaction may alter tertiary folding, making the protein less able to recover its original shape.

choices.r: Quaternary-structure trap: A protein with only one polypeptide has no quaternary structure or separate polypeptide subunits to pull apart. Its shape recovery can change through disruption of tertiary structure. Fix: Count the polypeptides before proposing that subunit separation causes the functional change.
choices.t: The replacement disrupts quaternary structure by separating polypeptide subunits, preventing the protein from recovering its original shape.

stem: A single-chain protein used in an elastic material returns to its original shape after gentle stretching. An ionic interaction between two R groups helps stabilize its folded form. Researchers produce a version in which one of these charged amino acids is replaced by an amino acid with a nonpolar R group; chain length and peptide-bond connectivity are unchanged. Which prediction best explains how this replacement could affect the protein’s shape recovery?
subject: biology

choices.r: Cell-type confusion: Prokaryotic cells have plasma membranes, even though they typically lack membrane-bound organelles. An enclosed cell does not need to be eukaryotic to contribute a membrane. Fix: Distinguish having a plasma membrane from having membrane-bound organelles.
choices.t: Double membranes indicate that the enclosed ancestors were eukaryotic rather than prokaryotic cells.

choices.r: Enclosure provides a way for an ancestral cell’s membrane to lie inside a surrounding host-derived membrane. Thus, double membranes support the model of an endosymbiotic origin for mitochondria and chloroplasts.
choices.t: Double membranes are consistent with a host cell enclosing an already membrane-bound prokaryotic cell.

choices.r: Membrane-folding substitution: This explanation replaces the model’s incorporation of a separate cell with rearrangement of the host’s own membrane. It omits the free-living prokaryotic ancestor central to endosymbiosis. Fix: Trace whether the model’s organelle begins as a separate cell or host membrane.
choices.t: Double membranes indicate that these organelles formed solely from folds of the host cell’s membrane.

choices.r: Overgeneralization: Evidence about mitochondria and chloroplasts does not establish the ancestry of every membrane-bound organelle. The model explains the endosymbiotic origin of these two organelle types. Fix: Limit the ancestry claim to the organelles represented by the model.
choices.t: Double membranes establish that every membrane-bound organelle descended from a free-living prokaryotic cell.

stem: A simplified model shows a host cell enclosing a free-living prokaryotic cell, which persists inside the host and eventually becomes an organelle. Mitochondria and chloroplasts both have double membranes. Which explanation best connects this structural feature to the evolutionary process represented by the model?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct. Greater species richness typically means more functional redundancy -- multiple species can fill similar ecological roles -- so losing any one species is less likely to eliminate a function from the community. This directly matches the CED principle that less diverse ecosystems are less resilient to change.
choices.t: As more species establish on the island, the community gains a wider range of ecological roles and more overlap in those roles between species, so the loss of any single species is less likely to collapse the whole community, matching the principle that less diverse ecosystems are less resilient to disturbance

choices.r: Incorrect. Ecosystem resilience is a property of the living community's structure, not just the substrate's physical stability; species richness is a recognized driver of ecosystem resilience.
choices.t: Species richness has no effect on how the island community responds to future disturbance, since resilience depends only on the physical stability of the volcanic rock itself, not on which organisms are present

choices.r: Incorrect. Resilience is not simply a function of total biomass -- a community with high biomass concentrated in very few species is more vulnerable to collapse if that species is lost, since redundancy across species, not just biomass, is what buffers against disturbance.
choices.t: Because each new species that arrives directly increases the total biomass of producers on the island, the ecosystem becomes more resilient simply by having more total organic matter available, regardless of how many species are present

choices.r: Incorrect. A single-species community has essentially no functional redundancy and would be highly vulnerable to any disturbance that specifically affects that one species -- the opposite of what makes a community resilient.
choices.t: The island becomes more resilient because later-arriving species outcompete and eliminate all earlier colonizers, leaving a single, well-adapted species that can withstand any future disturbance alone

stem: Based on the pattern of colonization described, which best explains why increasing species richness on the island over time is expected to make the resulting community more resilient to future disturbance?
stimulus: A volcanic eruption creates a new island of bare basalt with no soil. Over the following centuries, ecologists document how the community of organisms on the island changes. The first organisms to colonize the bare rock are cyanobacteria and lichens. As organic matter and soil accumulate, additional species -- mosses, ferns, small shrubs, and eventually a diverse mix of forest species -- establish themselves, and overall species richness on the island increases. The time scale spans decades to centuries.
subject: biology

choices.r: Energy-only misconception: Measuring stored starch addresses carbohydrate storage, not structural support. It does not determine whether removing cellulose changes tissue strength. Fix: Match the measured outcome to structural support by choosing a measure of strength.
choices.t: Randomly assign equal-sized strips from the same plant tissue to the treatment or an otherwise identical control solution, then compare the amount of starch stored in the strips.

choices.r: Confounded-variable trap: Strip thickness differs along with treatment and can affect tearing force. A strength difference therefore cannot be attributed specifically to cellulose removal. Fix: Keep strip dimensions equal across treatment and control groups.
choices.t: Apply the treatment to thin strips and an otherwise identical control solution to thick strips from the same plant tissue, then compare the force required to tear them.

choices.r: Missing-control trap: Averaging treated strips estimates their strength but provides no comparison showing whether cellulose removal changed it. Repeated measurements do not replace a control group. Fix: Include matched strips exposed to the same conditions without the cellulose-removing agent.
choices.t: Apply the treatment to all equal-sized strips from the same plant tissue, then measure the force required to tear each strip and calculate the average.

choices.r: Cellulose is a polysaccharide with a structural role in plants, so tearing force is a relevant measure of support. Matched strips and a control solution help isolate the effect of cellulose removal on tissue strength.
choices.t: Randomly assign equal-sized strips from the same plant tissue to the treatment or an otherwise identical solution without the cellulose-removing agent, then compare the force required to tear the strips.

stem: A researcher wants to test whether cellulose contributes to structural support in plant tissue. A treatment selectively removes cellulose without removing starch or other polysaccharides. Which experimental design best tests this question?
subject: biology

choices.r: The Calvin cycle uses chemical energy carried by ATP and NADPH, not light directly, and the 3-PGA level would rise and not fall.
choices.t: Both fall, because the Calvin cycle needs light directly to absorb energy.

choices.r: Correct: rubisco keeps making 3-PGA, but without ATP and NADPH from the light reactions the reduction of 3-PGA and the regeneration of RuBP stop, so 3-PGA accumulates and RuBP is depleted.
choices.t: 3-PGA rises and RuBP falls, because ATP and NADPH are no longer being made to reduce 3-PGA and regenerate RuBP.

choices.r: This is the pattern after removal of CO₂ in the light, and the stem says the CO₂ supply is constant.
choices.t: 3-PGA falls and RuBP rises, because carbon is no longer being fixed.

choices.r: The Calvin cycle is light independent only in that it does not absorb light, but it relies on the products of the light reactions, so its intermediates change.
choices.t: Neither changes, because the Calvin cycle is independent of light.

stem: A culture of green algae is photosynthesizing steadily in bright light with a constant supply of CO₂. The light is switched off, and over the next 30 seconds the cells are sampled and the concentrations of the Calvin cycle intermediates 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) are measured. Which change is most likely, assuming CO₂ fixation by rubisco continues briefly?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: The data show maximum liquid density at 4°C and a lower density for ice; the hydrogen-bonded open lattice of ice explains why it floats and leaves liquid water beneath.
choices.t: In ice each molecule is held in an open lattice by stable hydrogen bonds, which makes ice less dense so it floats and insulates the water below, while 4°C water is densest and sinks to the bottom.

choices.r: Ice has the most stable hydrogen bonds, not the fewest, and the 4°C water is denser because the molecules are closer together.
choices.t: Water at 4°C has the fewest hydrogen bonds, so it moves downward, and ice forms where bonds are fewest.

choices.r: Freezing does not break hydrogen bonds; it makes them more stable and fixed, and this explanation reverses the real cause of the lower density.
choices.t: Ice is less dense because its hydrogen bonds break, spreading the molecules apart, and the surface freezes first because the air is colder.

choices.r: The density data show that water is densest at 4°C and becomes less dense below that, so the coldest water does not sink to the bottom.
choices.t: All water becomes denser as it cools, so the coldest water stays at the bottom and the fish freeze first.

stem: A pond is monitored through a winter. The density of water is 0.9997 g/mL at 10°C, 1.0000 g/mL at 4°C, 0.9999 g/mL at 1°C, and 0.9998 g/mL for liquid water at 0°C. Ice at 0°C has a density of 0.917 g/mL. In midwinter the pond has a layer of ice at the surface, water near 0°C just under the ice, and water at 4°C at the bottom. Which statement best explains the layering and why the fish can survive?
subject: biology

choices.r: Additional carbon–carbon double bonds introduce kinks that limit tight packing, making the fats more liquid at the comparison temperature. This structural change neither makes the fats water-soluble nor changes their role as energy reserves.
choices.t: The reserves become more liquid but remain hydrophobic fats that store energy.

choices.r: Reversed packing effect: This prediction assumes that greater unsaturation allows fatty acid chains to pack more closely. Double-bond kinks interfere with close packing, favoring increased rather than decreased liquidity. Fix: Sketch straight and kinked chains, then compare how closely they can pack.
choices.t: The reserves become less liquid but remain hydrophobic fats that store energy.

choices.r: Liquid–soluble confusion: This prediction treats becoming liquid as becoming water-soluble. Unsaturated fats remain hydrophobic and can still function as energy reserves. Fix: Check whether the change affects packing, water solubility, or both.
choices.t: The reserves become more liquid and dissolve in water, losing their energy-storage role.

choices.r: Lipid-class interchangeability: This prediction incorrectly turns a change within stored fats into a change of lipid class. Increasing unsaturation does not create phospholipids or transfer their bilayer-forming function to fats. Fix: Name the lipid class before predicting whether its biological role changes.
choices.t: The reserves become more liquid and assemble into phospholipid bilayers, replacing their energy-storage role.

stem: A soil fungus exposed to a new growth condition replaces some saturated fatty acids in its stored fats with unsaturated fatty acids. Measurements show no change in total stored-fat mass or fatty acid chain length. Compared with reserves produced under the original condition, what change in the properties and function of these fats is most likely at an identical temperature?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Chromosome separation succeeded (two nuclei form), while cytoplasmic division failed, so actin is required for cytokinesis but not for spindle-based chromosome movement.
choices.t: Actin filaments form the contractile ring that divides the cytoplasm, and this step is separate from chromosome separation.

choices.r: Chromosomes separated normally in the treated cells, so this step does not depend on actin.
choices.t: Chromosome separation depends on actin filaments rather than on the spindle.

choices.r: The spindle is made of microtubules and formed normally even though actin polymerization was blocked.
choices.t: The spindle is made of actin, and its normal formation caused the two nuclei.

choices.r: The observed defect is failure to divide the cytoplasm, not a failure of vesicle delivery, which the data do not measure.
choices.t: Actin filaments carry vesicles to the plasma membrane, so vesicle delivery stopped.

stem: A drug blocks actin polymerization in dividing cultured cells but leaves microtubules unaffected. Treated cells form normal spindles and separate their chromosomes into two nuclei, but the cell does not pinch in two, and many cells end up with two nuclei. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: The ribosome-studded vesicles are rough ER, and the sacs that modify and sort proteins are the Golgi complex, so these two are swapped.
choices.t: Fraction 2, Golgi complex; fraction 3, rough ER; fraction 4, lysosomes.

choices.r: Correct: Ribosome-studded vesicles making proteins are rough ER; stacked sacs that modify and sort proteins are the Golgi complex; granules that store finished enzymes for release are secretory granules.
choices.t: Fraction 2, rough ER; fraction 3, Golgi complex; fraction 4, secretory granules.

choices.r: Stacked sacs that modify and sort proteins are the Golgi complex, and granules that store enzymes for release are secretory granules, so these two are swapped.
choices.t: Fraction 2, rough ER; fraction 3, secretory granules; fraction 4, Golgi complex.

choices.r: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion and are not described as releasing their contents when the cell is stimulated.
choices.t: Fraction 2, rough ER; fraction 3, Golgi complex; fraction 4, lysosomes.

stem: Pancreatic tissue is homogenized and separated into four fractions. Fraction 1 contains most of the DNA. Fraction 2 consists of closed vesicles studded with ribosomes on the outside that synthesize digestive enzyme precursors. Fraction 3 consists of stacked, flattened sacs that attach carbohydrate groups to proteins and sort them. Fraction 4 consists of membrane-bound granules packed with finished digestive enzymes that are released when the cell is stimulated. Which assignment is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Comparison reversal: Water's temperature increases by 2°C, not 10°C. Its smaller increase under equal heating and equal mass indicates a higher specific heat capacity than liquid X. Fix: Subtract each liquid's initial temperature from its final temperature before comparing increases.
choices.t: Water shows a larger temperature increase, indicating a lower specific heat capacity than liquid X.

choices.r: Bond-type confusion: This explanation substitutes bonds within water molecules for attractions between molecules. Water's high specific heat capacity involves disruption of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not breaking its O–H covalent bonds. Fix: Identify whether the bonds in your explanation connect separate molecules or atoms within one molecule.
choices.t: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because added energy breaks covalent bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen atoms.

choices.r: Water warms by 2°C while liquid X warms by 10°C under equal heating. Water's polarity enables hydrogen bonding, and disrupting these attractions absorbs energy, contributing to its high specific heat capacity. This property helps stabilize temperatures in organisms and aquatic environments.
choices.t: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because some added energy disrupts hydrogen bonds between its polar molecules.

choices.r: Neutral-means-nonpolar misconception: Water has no net charge, but its charge distribution is uneven, making it polar. Its molecules form hydrogen bonds; the absence of these attractions does not explain its high specific heat capacity. Fix: Check charge distribution within a molecule rather than using net charge to determine polarity.
choices.t: Water shows a smaller temperature increase because its nonpolar molecules do not form hydrogen bonds.

stem:
A researcher adds equal amounts of heat to equal masses of water and liquid X during each heating interval. Neither liquid evaporates, and no heat escapes to the surroundings.

Temperature data:
Heating intervals completed | Water (°C) | Liquid X (°C)
0 | 20 | 20
1 | 21 | 25
2 | 22 | 30

Which statement best describes the temperature pattern and explains the molecular basis of water's response?
subject: biology

choices.r: The mutant cyclin builds up like the normal one and activates CDK1, so entry into mitosis is not blocked.
choices.t: The cells never enter mitosis, because CDK1 cannot be activated by the mutant cyclin.

choices.r: Correct: cyclin B rises normally, so CDK1 activates and the cells enter mitosis; without degradation of cyclin B, CDK1 stays active and mitosis cannot be completed.
choices.t: The cells enter mitosis normally but cannot complete it, because CDK1 activity stays high after anaphase.

choices.r: High cyclin B and CDK1 activity keep cells in mitosis, and they do not move into a new round of replication.
choices.t: The cells skip mitosis and begin another round of DNA replication, because cyclin B is present.

choices.r: CDK1 is constant, and its activity depends on cyclin B, so the cyclin level controls timing.
choices.t: The cells divide normally, because the amount of CDK1 and not the amount of cyclin sets the timing.

stem: In dividing cells, the concentration of the kinase CDK1 stays constant. Cyclin B accumulates during G2, peaks at metaphase, and falls sharply at anaphase. CDK1 kinase activity rises and falls with the amount of cyclin B. A mutant cyclin B cannot be degraded. Which outcome is most likely in cells that make only the mutant cyclin B?
subject: biology

choices.r: The bilayer’s hydrophobic interior presents a barrier to charged Cl⁻ but permits small, nonpolar N₂ to pass directly. Disabling transport proteins therefore restricts chloride passage without preventing nitrogen passage.
choices.t: Cl⁻ passage is strongly restricted, while N₂ crosses readily because it can pass through the hydrophobic interior.

choices.r: Size-only trap: This prediction overlooks charge as a determinant of permeability. Although Cl⁻ is small, its charge strongly restricts passage through the hydrophobic interior. Fix: Check each particle’s charge and polarity before using size to predict permeability.
choices.t: Cl⁻ and N₂ both cross readily because their small size allows them through the bilayer.

choices.r: Surface-only trap: This prediction treats the membrane’s surfaces as the only barrier. Particles must also traverse the hydrophobic interior, which restricts charged Cl⁻ rather than small, nonpolar N₂. Fix: Follow each particle’s path through both surfaces and the bilayer interior.
choices.t: Cl⁻ crosses readily, while N₂ passage is strongly restricted because the membrane’s outer surfaces are hydrophilic.

choices.r: Universal protein requirement trap: This prediction incorrectly extends the need for transport proteins to every substance. Small, nonpolar N₂ can cross the lipid bilayer without a protein pathway. Fix: Identify whether each substance can cross the hydrophobic interior directly before requiring a protein.
choices.t: Cl⁻ and N₂ are both strongly restricted because crossing the membrane always requires functioning transport proteins.

stem: An experimental treatment disables transport proteins in a freshwater alga’s plasma membrane but leaves its phospholipid bilayer intact. Nitrogen gas (N₂) consists of small, nonpolar molecules, whereas chloride (Cl⁻) is a small, charged ion. After treatment, which prediction about passage through this membrane is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Removal requires dissolving the bilayer, so the protein is not simply attached outside, and nonpolar stretches would not face water.
choices.t: A protein attached to the outside of the membrane, with its nonpolar stretches facing the watery fluid around it.

choices.r: Nonpolar stretches facing water are unstable, and the need for detergent shows Protein T is part of the bilayer, not dissolved.
choices.t: A protein dissolved in the cytoplasm, with its nonpolar stretches facing outward toward the surrounding water.

choices.r: Polar regions are not stable among the hydrophobic tails; the nonpolar stretches belong there.
choices.t: A protein with all of its polar regions buried in the center of the bilayer, among the hydrophobic tails.

choices.r: Nonpolar stretches fit among the hydrophobic tails, while polar regions stay in the aqueous environments on either side.
choices.t: A protein that crosses the bilayer several times, with its nonpolar stretches in the membrane interior and its polar regions outside the bilayer.

stem: A researcher determines the amino acid sequence of Protein T. Seven separate stretches of about 20 amino acids each have only nonpolar R groups, and the regions between the stretches have mostly polar R groups. Protein T can be removed from membranes only by dissolving the lipid bilayer with a detergent. Which description of Protein T is best supported by these results?
subject: biology

choices.r: Each five-monomer linear chain has 4 bonds, so building three chains takes 12 dehydration reactions and releases 12 water molecules. Each hydrolysis consumes one water and adds one molecule, giving 3 + 4 = 7 molecules and a net release of 12 − 4 = 8 water molecules.
choices.t: Seven separate molecules; eight water molecules released overall.

choices.r: Water-total addition error: this treats both bond formation and bond cleavage as releasing water. The 12 dehydration reactions release water, but the 4 hydrolysis reactions consume it. Fix: Subtract the water consumed by hydrolysis from the water released by dehydration synthesis.
choices.t: Seven separate molecules; sixteen water molecules released overall.

choices.r: Water-direction reversal: this flips the sign of the net change. Dehydration synthesis released 12 water molecules while hydrolysis used only 4, so release exceeds consumption. Fix: Place water as a product for dehydration synthesis and as a reactant for hydrolysis before totaling.
choices.t: Seven separate molecules; eight water molecules consumed overall.

choices.r: Bond-count versus fragment-count error: this equates the number of bonds broken with the number of molecules present. The cell already had three chains, and each cleavage adds one more molecule to that count. Fix: Start from the number of chains and add one molecule for each bond hydrolyzed.
choices.t: Four separate molecules; eight water molecules released overall.

stem: A plant cell starts with fifteen free monomers and uses dehydration synthesis to assemble them into three separate linear chains of five monomers each. An enzyme then hydrolyzes exactly four monomer-linking bonds, chosen anywhere among the three chains. No other bonds form or break. Compared with the fifteen free monomers at the start, how many separate molecules result, and what is the net change in water molecules?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Ends increase from about 667 to about 1,333, which is a factor of two, so the release rate roughly doubles.
choices.t: It roughly doubles, in proportion to the number of ends.

choices.r: More branches means more ends, so the release rate rises rather than falls.
choices.t: It is halved, because shorter branches hold less glucose.

choices.r: Total glucose is unchanged but rate depends on the number of ends.
choices.t: It is unchanged, because the same 8,000 units are present.

choices.r: Halving the spacing doubles the number of ends, so the rate changes by a factor of about two, not six.
choices.t: It rises about sixfold, because the spacing changed from 12 to 6 units.

stem: A polysaccharide of 8,000 glucose units has a branch about every 12 units (about 667 chain ends). A mutation shortens the spacing to a branch about every 6 units (about 1,333 chain ends). If an enzyme removes glucose from ends at a constant rate per end, how does the initial release rate change?
subject: biology

choices.r: Volume-for-surface substitution: This uses unchanged cell volume to infer unchanged capacity for membrane-associated reactions. Here, enzyme number depends on internal membrane area, which decreases. Fix: Determine whether enzyme number depends on membrane area or cell volume.
choices.t: The compartment can support the same number of simultaneous reactions because the cell’s volume has not changed.

choices.r: Internal–external membrane confusion: This treats the compartment’s membrane as the cell’s external boundary. Plasma membrane area remains unchanged, so the internal area reduction does not remove surface for external exchange. Fix: Identify which membrane contacts the surroundings before predicting nutrient uptake.
choices.t: The cell takes up nutrients more slowly because smoothing the internal folds reduces its surface area for exchange with the surroundings.

choices.r: The internal membrane provides attachment surfaces for the reaction enzymes. Halving its area while maintaining the same enzyme density halves the number of attached enzymes, reducing the capacity for simultaneous reactions.
choices.t: The compartment can support fewer simultaneous reactions because the smaller internal membrane area accommodates fewer enzymes.

choices.r: Folding-means-less-area misconception: This assumes that removing folds creates more membrane surface. The stated area instead decreases from 60 μm² to 30 μm², leaving room for fewer attached enzymes. Fix: Compare total membrane areas before inferring how folding affects enzyme capacity.
choices.t: The compartment can support more simultaneous reactions because smoothing the folds increases the membrane area available for enzymes.

stem:
A computer simulation models a membrane-bound compartment in a yeast cell. Enzymes attached to the compartment’s membrane carry out metabolic reactions. A remodeling step smooths out membrane folds, reducing total internal membrane area from 60 μm² to 30 μm². Cell volume and plasma membrane area remain unchanged. The number of attached enzymes per unit membrane area stays constant, and reactants remain abundant.

Which prediction best explains how remodeling affects the cell’s function?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: A = T = 18%, so A + T = 36%; the remaining 64% is G + C, with G = C, so cytosine is 32%.
18% is the percentage of thymine and adenine, and cytosine pairs with guanine rather than thymine.
64% is the total of G plus C, and cytosine is only half of this.
82% is 100 minus thymine and does not account for the pairing of A with T.

stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA from a fish is found to contain 18% thymine. What percentage of the bases is cytosine?
subject: biology

choices.r: Stabilizing selection would maintain intermediate beak sizes and reduce the frequency of both extremes — the opposite of what is observed. The data show a bimodal distribution (two peaks, few intermediates), which is the signature of disruptive selection or character displacement, not stabilizing selection.
choices.t: Stabilizing selection is acting to maintain intermediate beak sizes because intermediate beaks represent a compromise between the two seed types

choices.r: Disruptive (diversifying) selection acts when both phenotypic extremes have higher fitness than the intermediate. Here: small beaks fit small seeds; large beaks fit large seeds; intermediate beaks are poor at both, giving them the lowest fitness. Differential survival and reproduction favors both extremes, generating and maintaining the observed bimodal distribution over time.
choices.t: Disruptive selection is favoring birds with extreme beak sizes (small thin or large thick) because each extreme specializes efficiently on one seed type, while intermediate beaks are inefficient at both resources — reducing fitness of intermediates relative to both extremes

choices.r: Directional selection would shift the mean in one direction, producing a unimodal distribution that moves over time. The bimodal distribution (two phenotypic peaks) is not consistent with directional selection, which would eliminate small beaks, not maintain them alongside large beaks.
choices.t: Directional selection is shifting the entire population toward large beak size because large seeds provide more calories per seed

choices.r: There is no information given about mate choice or sexual selection. The explanation provided in the stimulus (beak efficiency on different seed types) is ecological — it invokes natural selection based on foraging efficiency and food availability, not sexual selection based on mate preferences.
choices.t: Sexual selection is the primary driver, with females preferring extreme beak sizes because intermediates are visually less attractive

stem: Which scenario best explains the beak polymorphism observed in this bird population?
stimulus: A population of seed-eating finches on an island feeds on two types of seeds: very small soft seeds and very large hard seeds. Birds with small thin beaks can efficiently crack small seeds but cannot crack large seeds. Birds with large thick beaks can efficiently crack large seeds but are inefficient at handling small seeds. Birds with intermediate beaks are poor at cracking both seed types. Data collected over 20 years show a bimodal distribution of beak size with few birds in the intermediate range.
subject: biology

choices.r: Tempting if you assume any protein makes transport passive. But direction matters: moving up a gradient costs energy no matter which protein helps. Fix: first find the gradient direction.
choices.t: It is passive transport, because a membrane protein is involved and proteins lower the energy needed.

choices.r: Tempting because charged ions do need proteins to cross. But facilitated diffusion only moves substances down their gradient, and here the ion moves up it. Fix: channels explain how, gradient direction explains energy.
choices.t: It is facilitated diffusion, because ions are charged and charged particles always use channels.

choices.r: Net movement against the concentration gradient is active transport. The cell must supply energy, usually ATP, to move the ion toward the side where it is already more concentrated.
choices.t: It is active transport, because the ion moves from low to high concentration, which requires energy input, typically from ATP.

choices.r: Tempting because endocytosis also uses energy. But endocytosis moves bulk material in vesicles, and here a single protein moves one ion. Fix: pumps move individual ions against gradients; vesicles move large particles.
choices.t: It is endocytosis, because transport against a gradient is always done in vesicles.

stem: The concentration of an ion is 140 mM inside a cell and 4 mM outside. A membrane protein moves the ion into the cell. Which statement best describes this movement?
subject: biology

choices.r: Alternative splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple mRNA and protein isoforms.
choices.t: Each gene can produce only one protein, so proteome complexity cannot exceed gene count.

choices.r: Because one exon is chosen independently from each of the three groups, many different exon combinations are possible from a single gene, each yielding a distinct mRNA and potentially a distinct protein. This is why the proteome can exceed the genome's gene count.
choices.t: Selecting one exon independently from each of the three alternative-exon groups creates many different possible exon combinations, so a single gene can encode multiple distinct protein isoforms

choices.r: Alternative splicing produces multiple mRNAs from one pre-mRNA transcribed from a single promoter and a single gene copy. No duplication of promoters or gene copies is needed -- this confuses splicing-based diversity with gene duplication.
choices.t: Each of the 12 possible isoforms requires its own separate promoter and its own copy of the gene

choices.r: Different exon combinations change the mRNA's coding sequence, which changes the resulting protein's amino acid sequence. The 5' cap structure is chemically identical across all of a cell's mRNAs regardless of which exons were included -- this gets the mechanism backwards.
choices.t: The 12 isoforms differ only in which 5' cap structure they carry, not in their amino acid sequence

stem: How does alternative splicing allow proteome complexity to exceed the number of genes in a genome?
stimulus: A single gene contains three groups of alternative exons. One exon is selected from each group when the pre-mRNA is spliced. The groups contain 2, 3, and 2 possible exons, respectively.
subject: biology

choices.r: This reverses the assignments, since cellulase cuts beta-1,4 links and amylase cuts alpha-1,4 links.
choices.t: P has alpha-1,4 linkages and Q has beta-1,4 linkages.

choices.r: Identical monomers do not mean identical structure, as the different enzyme results show different linkages.
choices.t: P and Q have identical structures, because both are made only of glucose.

choices.r: The stem states both are made only of glucose, so the monomers are the same.
choices.t: P and Q differ because P contains a different monomer than Q.

choices.r: Correct: Each enzyme cuts one linkage orientation, so the opposite results show that the two polymers have different glycosidic linkages despite identical monomers.
choices.t: P has beta-1,4 linkages like cellulose and Q has alpha-1,4 linkages like starch, so they differ in linkage orientation.

stem: Two unknown polymers, P and Q, are each made only of glucose. Polymer P is hydrolyzed by cellulase but not by amylase. Polymer Q is hydrolyzed by amylase but not by cellulase. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: The enzymes digest the cellulose wall, not the plasma membrane, which still bounds the protoplast.
choices.t: Protoplasts lose their plasma membranes during digestion, so distilled water flows freely through them until they rupture.

choices.r: Distilled water is hypotonic to both intact cells and protoplasts; the wall, not an isotonic cytoplasm, prevents bursting.
choices.t: Intact cells stay whole because their cytoplasm is isotonic to distilled water, whereas the protoplasts become hypotonic to it.

choices.r: The wall provides counter-pressure that limits swelling in intact cells; removing it lets water entry continue until the membrane lyses.
choices.t: Without a wall, protoplasts have nothing to resist water entering by osmosis, so no turgor pressure limits swelling and the membrane ruptures.

choices.r: Water moving out would shrink the cells; bursting results from net water entry in a hypotonic solution.
choices.t: The enzyme treatment makes the cytoplasm of protoplasts hypertonic to the intact cells, so water moves out until they burst.

stem: Plant biologists treat leaf cells with enzymes that digest the cellulose cell wall, producing protoplasts. Intact leaf cells placed in distilled water become firm but stay intact, whereas protoplasts placed in distilled water swell and many burst. Which best explains the difference in outcome?
subject: biology

choices.r: Cell-type confusion: A plasma membrane is not exclusive to eukaryotes; prokaryotes also possess one despite typically lacking membrane-bound organelles. Two surrounding membranes therefore do not require a eukaryotic ancestor. Fix: Check whether you are identifying a cell boundary or an internal membrane-bound organelle.
choices.t: The mitochondrial membranes indicate that the incorporated ancestor was a eukaryotic cell rather than a prokaryotic cell.

choices.r: Membrane-folding substitution: Rearranging only the host membrane leaves out the independent prokaryotic ancestor central to endosymbiotic theory. It substitutes a different origin for the one the question asks you to explain. Fix: Trace whether the proposed ancestor is an independent cell or part of the host.
choices.t: The mitochondrial membranes support an origin entirely through folding of the host membrane, without incorporating a separate cell.

choices.r: Overgeneralization: A model explaining mitochondrial ancestry does not establish the same ancestry for every membrane-bound organelle. Endosymbiotic theory accounts for mitochondria and chloroplasts, not all internal compartments. Fix: Match the scope of your ancestry claim to the organelles the evidence addresses.
choices.t: The mitochondrial membranes demonstrate that all membrane-bound organelles originated through the incorporation of free-living prokaryotic cells.

choices.r: Surrounding an already membrane-bounded cell with a host membrane provides a model for two nested membranes. This arrangement supports the proposed origin of mitochondria from free-living prokaryotes through endosymbiosis.
choices.t: The mitochondrial membranes are consistent with a host membrane surrounding an ancestral prokaryotic cell that already had a plasma membrane.

stem: A biology class compares a computer model of a bacterium with a cross-sectional model of a mitochondrion from a mouse cell. The bacterial model includes a plasma membrane, while the mitochondrial model shows two surrounding membranes. Which explanation best connects these models to endosymbiotic theory?
subject: biology

choices.r: Moving the solute against its concentration gradient requires energy input. Breaking the coupling prevents energy released by ATP hydrolysis from driving that movement, despite continued ATP availability and hydrolysis.
choices.t: Uphill transport slows because ATP hydrolysis no longer supplies energy through coupling to the transport process.

choices.r: The energy-release-equals-coupling misconception assumes that releasing energy anywhere automatically powers a particular process. Continued ATP hydrolysis cannot drive uphill transport when their coupling is broken. Fix: Trace the coupling between the energy-releasing reaction and the transport process.
choices.t: Uphill transport proceeds at its previous rate because ATP hydrolysis elsewhere automatically provides the energy for transport.

choices.r: The catalysis-versus-energy misconception mistakes lowering activation energy for supplying energy. Catalytic activity does not remove the energy requirement for moving a solute against its gradient. Fix: Distinguish lowering activation energy from providing energy for uphill transport.
choices.t: Uphill transport proceeds at its previous rate because the protein's catalytic activity removes the need for energy input.

choices.r: The reversed-energy-flow misconception incorrectly assigns a net energy cost to ATP hydrolysis. Under cellular conditions, ATP hydrolysis releases energy; the transport slowdown results from losing coupling, not from hydrolysis consuming that energy. Fix: Mark which process releases energy and which process requires energy input.
choices.t: Uphill transport slows because ATP hydrolysis consumes energy that would otherwise power solute movement.

stem: A yeast cell uses a membrane protein to move an uncharged solute against its concentration gradient, powered by coupled ATP hydrolysis. A treatment disconnects ATP hydrolysis from transport without altering the protein's catalytic activity. During the observation, ATP concentration, the solute gradient, and the ATP hydrolysis rate are maintained; no replacement energy source is coupled to transport. What immediate effect on uphill solute transport is expected, and why?
subject: biology

choices.r: The values must be added with their signs, and adding magnitudes treats an energy cost as a gain.
choices.t: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −50 kJ/mol, because the two magnitudes add.

choices.r: Correct: the free-energy changes of coupled reactions add algebraically, +20 + (−30) = −10 kJ/mol, which is negative, so the overall process is spontaneous.
choices.t: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of −10 kJ/mol, so it can proceed spontaneously.

choices.r: Coupling changes the overall free-energy change because the ATP hydrolysis is part of the coupled reaction.
choices.t: The coupled reaction keeps a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol, so it still does not proceed.

choices.r: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic and contributes a negative value, so it lowers the total and does not raise it.
choices.t: The coupled reaction has a free-energy change of +50 kJ/mol, because the ATP hydrolysis adds a cost.

stem: A cell converts compound X to compound Y in a reaction with a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol. The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate has a free-energy change of −30 kJ/mol. An enzyme couples the two by transferring the terminal phosphate of ATP to X. Which prediction is best?
subject: biology

choices.r: Uptake per unit area is constant, but total demand grows with volume and outpaces total uptake once r exceeds 12 micrometers.
choices.t: Supply stays above demand, because supply per square micrometer does not change as the cell grows.

choices.r: A ratio of one half would occur at r = 24, not at r = 15.
choices.t: Supply falls from twice the demand to exactly half of the demand.

choices.r: Correct: At r = 6 the ratio is 12/6 = 2.0; at r = 15 it is 12/15 = 0.80, so supply falls from twice the demand to 80% of it.
choices.t: Supply falls from twice the demand to 80% of the demand.

choices.r: Total surface area does rise, but volume rises faster, so the cell can meet demand only up to r = 12 micrometers.
choices.t: Supply rises with the larger surface area, so the cell can meet demand at any radius.

stem: A growing spherical cell is modeled as follows. Nutrient uptake is 2.0 units per square micrometer of surface per minute, and nutrient use is 0.5 units per cubic micrometer of cytoplasm per minute. For a sphere, surface area is 4πr² and volume is (4/3)πr³. For this model, supply divided by demand equals 12 divided by r, with r in micrometers. What is predicted if the cell grows from a radius of 6 micrometers to 15 micrometers?
subject: biology

choices.r: The receptor acts upstream of Gs, and Gs is already locked in its active state, so blocking the receptor does not lower cAMP.
choices.t: cAMP stays high, and a receptor antagonist lowers it, because the receptor must keep activating Gs.

choices.r: Toxin-modified Gs stays active even with no hormone, so cAMP does not wait for the hormone.
choices.t: cAMP stays low until the hormone is added, because Gs cannot work without the receptor.

choices.r: In this pathway cAMP signals through PKA, so a PKA inhibitor blocks the response to high cAMP.
choices.t: cAMP stays high, but a PKA inhibitor has no effect on secretion, because cAMP acts independently of PKA.

choices.r: Correct: a Gs that cannot turn itself off keeps adenylyl cyclase active without receptor input; PKA lies downstream of cAMP, so only a PKA inhibitor can stop the secretion.
choices.t: cAMP stays high and chloride secretion continues, a receptor antagonist does not reduce it, and a PKA inhibitor does.

stem: In intestinal cells, a hormone binds a receptor that activates Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP. cAMP activates PKA, and PKA triggers chloride secretion. Cholera toxin modifies Gs so that it cannot break down its bound GTP and stays active. Cells are treated with the toxin and no hormone. Which result is predicted?
subject: biology

choices.r: Reaction-name reversal: the observed breakdown is assigned to a reaction that builds polymers. Dehydration synthesis joins monomers through covalent bond formation, so it cannot explain this breakdown. Fix: Identify bond formation or cleavage before choosing the reaction name.
choices.t: Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; dehydration synthesis releases water to cleave covalent bonds.

choices.r: Water-direction reversal: hydrolysis is identified appropriately, but water is incorrectly described as an output. Water is used in hydrolysis, supplying H and OH to the products of bond cleavage. Fix: Mark water as an input when writing a hydrolysis reaction.
choices.t: Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; hydrolysis produces water as it cleaves covalent bonds.

choices.r: Trend reversal: the proposed changes run opposite to the measurements. The sample loses nine intact chains and gains 72 unattached monomers rather than showing polymer assembly. Fix: Calculate the change from first to last measurement in each column.
choices.t: Intact chains become more numerous while unattached monomers disappear; dehydration synthesis releases water as it forms covalent bonds.

choices.r: Chain counts fall from 12 to 3 while unattached monomer counts rise from 0 to 72, indicating polymer breakdown. Hydrolysis accomplishes this by using water to split covalent bonds between monomers.
choices.t: Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; hydrolysis uses water to cleave covalent bonds.

stem:
A biodegradable coating contains biological polymer chains, each made of eight monomers connected by covalent bonds. During processing, a fixed sample of the coating gives these measurements:

Processing time (minutes) | Intact polymer chains | Unattached monomers
0 | 12 | 0
4 | 9 | 24
8 | 3 | 72

Which description connects the measured changes with the chemical reaction taking place?
subject: biology

choices.r: Lowering activation energy changes speed only, and the free-energy change that sets the equilibrium is unchanged.
choices.t: The enzyme makes the reaction spontaneous because it lowers the activation energy, so most X becomes Y.

choices.r: An enzyme does not shift the equilibrium, because it speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally and leaves the free-energy difference between X and Y unchanged.
choices.t: The enzyme speeds the approach to equilibrium and shifts the equilibrium toward Y, so at equilibrium most of the material is Y.

choices.r: Enzymes are not consumed and do not donate energy from their own bonds to drive reactions.
choices.t: The enzyme supplies energy from its own bonds, so the reaction proceeds until all X is gone.

choices.r: Correct: a catalyst changes the rate and not the free-energy change or the equilibrium position, so the reaction with ΔG = +20 kJ/mol still favors X.
choices.t: The enzyme speeds the approach to equilibrium, but at equilibrium most of the material is still X because the enzyme does not change the free-energy change.

stem: An enzyme is added to a solution of X, which converts to Y in a reaction with a free-energy change of +20 kJ/mol. No ATP is present. Which prediction about the reaction after a long time is best?
subject: biology

choices.r: A nuclear origin would predict mitochondrial genes most similar to nuclear genes, but the similarity to the nucleus is the lowest of the three.
choices.t: Mitochondria arose from the nucleus by infolding of the nuclear envelope.

choices.r: 55% is a lower similarity than the 80% shared with the bacterium, so the data do not point to an archaeal origin of mitochondria.
choices.t: Mitochondria are archaeal in origin, because 55% identity is the highest similarity to an archaeon.

choices.r: Correct: The mitochondrial sequence is much closer to a bacterial sequence (80%) than to the host nuclear sequence (52%) or an archaeal sequence (55%), the pattern predicted if mitochondria descended from a bacterium taken up by a host cell.
