choices.t: Mitochondrial genes are more similar to those of bacteria than to those of the host's nucleus, which supports an origin from an engulfed bacterium.

choices.r: The bacterium is a free-living cell, and the data cannot show that it came from an organelle; the usual direction is the reverse.
choices.t: The similarity is the result of the bacterium having been derived from mitochondria.

stem: A researcher compares the gene for ribosomal RNA found in the mitochondria of a yeast cell with three other sequences. The mitochondrial gene is 80% identical to the equivalent gene of a purple bacterium, 55% identical to the equivalent gene of an archaeon, and 52% identical to the yeast's own nuclear gene for ribosomal RNA. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Tempting because much ion movement is passive. But maintaining the gradients requires active transport by the pump, which depends on ATP. Fix: passive movement uses gradients, active transport builds them.
choices.t: Nothing changes, because ion movement across membranes is entirely passive because pumps are not needed to hold ions at different levels across a membrane.

choices.r: Tempting because the poison leaves the proteins intact. But the pump needs ATP to operate, not just an intact structure. Fix: an undamaged pump still needs its energy supply.
choices.t: The pumps keep working at the same rate, because the proteins themselves are undamaged.

choices.r: Tempting because ions would move down their gradients without ATP. But the pumps do not reverse; they simply stop, and any leaking happens through other pathways. Fix: no ATP means the pump halts.
choices.t: The pumps reverse direction and move Na+ in and K+ out by facilitated diffusion.

choices.r: The Na+/K+ pump is an ATPase that needs a steady supply of ATP to move ions against their gradients. Without ATP the pump fails, and the gradients and membrane potential it maintains cannot be sustained.
choices.t: The pumps stop moving Na+ out and K+ in against their gradients, so the gradients and membrane potential gradually dissipate.

stem: A poison stops a nerve cell's ATP production but does not damage its membrane proteins. Which is the most direct consequence for the cell's Na+/K+ pumps and ion gradients?
subject: biology

choices.r: Undamaged WT and mutated cells have the same percent in G1, so p53 does not change cycle speed on its own.
choices.t: p53 speeds up the cell cycle, because WT cells have more cells in G1.

choices.r: Cells in G0 would not be cycling, and 31% of the mutated cells are in S, so they keep dividing.
choices.t: The mutated cells are in G0 after UV exposure, because they show no change.

choices.r: Correct: without UV the two groups are the same, so p53 does not change the cycle by itself; after UV, only the WT cells raise p21 and arrest in G1, while mutated cells keep going into S phase.
choices.t: After DNA damage, p53 raises p21 and holds cells in G1; without p53, damaged cells continue into S phase.

choices.r: WT cells enter S phase far less after UV (4% against 30%), so they are held back and not helped to enter, and the data do not show repair.
choices.t: p53 repairs the UV damage directly, which allows the WT cells to enter S phase.

stem:
Cells with normal p53 (WT) and cells with a mutated p53 gene are grown, and half of each group is exposed to UV light that damages DNA. Twenty-four hours later, researchers measure the percent of cells in G1 and S and the level of p21 protein.
Cells | UV | In G1 | In S | p21 level
WT | no | 60% | 30% | low
WT | yes | 90% | 4% | high
Mutated p53 | no | 60% | 30% | low
Mutated p53 | yes | 58% | 31% | low
Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: If autosomal recessive, unaffected female II-4 would need genotype Cc. Her unaffected husband III-1 must also be Cc to produce affected son III-2. While this is possible, the consistent male-only expression across two generations (4 affected males, 0 affected females) strongly favors X-linkage. Autosomal would require two carriers marrying in both generations without any affected females.
choices.t: The gene is autosomal recessive; the pattern of only males being affected is coincidental in this small pedigree

choices.r: X-linked recessive explains all observations: (1) Males are affected (X^c Y hemizygous, no second X to provide dominant allele); (2) Females are unaffected carriers (X^C X^c — dominant allele on second X masks the recessive); (3) I-2 must be carrier (X^C X^c) because she has affected sons who received X^c from her; (4) II-4 inherited X^c from mother I-2, making her X^C X^c carrier, explaining her affected son III-2.
choices.t: The gene is X-linked recessive: males are hemizygous (\(X^{c}Y\)) and express the recessive allele without a dominant allele to mask it; carrier females (\(X^{C}X^{c}\)) are unaffected; unaffected mother I-2 is a carrier who passed \(X^{c}\) to her affected sons

choices.r: Y-linked traits appear in ALL sons of an affected father — but I-1 (the father) is unaffected while two of his sons (II-1, II-3) are affected. Y-linked inheritance requires an affected father. Since I-1 is unaffected, Y-linkage cannot explain the pattern.
choices.t: The gene is Y-linked; it passes directly from father to all sons

choices.r: X-linked dominant traits would affect females in each generation because a carrier mother (having one dominant allele) would be affected herself, not just a carrier. Additionally, X-linked dominant traits affect daughters of affected fathers 100% of the time. Neither feature matches this pedigree where all affected individuals are male and no females are affected.
choices.t: The gene is X-linked dominant; affected males inherited the dominant allele from their carrier mother

stem: Which statement about the inheritance of color blindness in this family is best supported by the pedigree?
stimulus:
A pedigree shows: Generation I — unaffected father (I-1) and unaffected mother (I-2). Generation II — three sons: II-1 color blind, II-2 unaffected, II-3 color blind; one daughter: II-4 unaffected. Generation III — II-4 married an unaffected man (III-1); their children are III-2 (son, color blind) and III-3 (daughter, unaffected).

Color blindness is caused by a recessive allele. The trait appears only in males in this pedigree.
subject: biology

choices.r: The uniform-mixing misconception assumes that mixing enzymes prevents interference. Mixing these enzyme groups would instead allow cytoplasmic enzymes greater access to Y, enabling its conversion back into X. Fix: Trace what each enzyme group would do if both occupied the same space.
choices.t: It spreads both groups of enzymes throughout the cytoplasm so their reactions cannot interfere with one another.

choices.r: The complete-isolation misconception treats a compartment as a sealed, independent system. Compartment membranes allow controlled exchange with the cell while maintaining separation between processes. Fix: Distinguish separating reactions from preventing all material exchange.
choices.t: It blocks every exchange of molecules with the cytoplasm so the compartment operates independently of the cell.

choices.r: The internal-versus-external surface-area confusion assigns an internal membrane the role of the cell’s outer boundary. This compartment membrane does not add plasma membrane surface for uptake from the environment. Fix: Identify the spaces on each side of the membrane before assigning its benefit.
choices.t: It enlarges the plasma membrane so the cell can absorb substances faster from its surroundings.

choices.r: The compartment provides a separate space for producing Y. Its membrane limits contact between Y inside the compartment and cytoplasmic enzymes that could reverse its production, reducing interference between the reactions.
choices.t: It separates the production of Y from cytoplasmic reactions that would convert Y back into X.

stem: In a yeast cell, enzymes inside a membrane-bound compartment convert substance X into substance Y. Enzymes in the cytoplasm can convert Y back into X. How does the compartment membrane benefit the production of Y?
subject: biology

choices.r: A G1 arrest would leave most cells at 3.0 pg, and only 6% are there.
choices.t: Drug D arrests cells in G1, before DNA replication begins.

choices.r: An S-phase arrest would leave most cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg, and only 9% are there.
choices.t: Drug D arrests cells during S phase, partway through DNA replication.

choices.r: Correct: most treated cells hold 6.0 pg, so they have completed S phase, and few are at 3.0 pg or in between; they stay at 6.0 pg until division, so they are arrested in G2 or M.
choices.t: Drug D lets cells replicate their DNA but arrests them in G2 or mitosis, before the cell divides.

choices.r: Cells in G0 have not replicated their DNA and would hold 3.0 pg.
choices.t: Drug D makes cells leave the cycle and enter G0, in which they hold 6.0 pg of DNA.

stem:
A cultured cell line has 3.0 pg of DNA per cell in G1 and 6.0 pg after DNA replication is complete, until the cell divides. Flow cytometry measures DNA per cell.
Sample | Cells at 3.0 pg | Cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg | Cells at 6.0 pg
Untreated | 52% | 18% | 30%
24 hours with drug D | 6% | 9% | 85%
Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: The energy-release-equals-coupling misconception treats energy released elsewhere as automatically available for cellular work. The synthesis reaction needs coupling, not merely simultaneous ATP hydrolysis. Fix: Check whether the energy-releasing reaction is actually coupled to the energy-requiring process.
choices.t: Polymer synthesis remains unchanged because ATP hydrolysis anywhere in the cell supplies the energy needed for synthesis.

choices.r: Polymer synthesis requires energy input. Disrupting coupling prevents ATP hydrolysis from powering that reaction, even though ATP remains available and hydrolysis continues.
choices.t: Polymer synthesis decreases because energy released by ATP hydrolysis is no longer coupled to the energy-requiring synthesis reaction.

choices.r: The catalysis-versus-energy misconception confuses lowering activation energy with supplying energy for a reaction. Enzymes do not eliminate polymer synthesis's energy requirement. Fix: Separate the enzyme's effect on activation energy from the reaction's need for energy input.
choices.t: Polymer synthesis remains unchanged because its enzymes eliminate the need for energy input.

choices.r: The reversed-energy-flow misconception treats ATP hydrolysis as a net energy-consuming process. Under cellular conditions, ATP hydrolysis releases energy; synthesis decreases here because coupling is disrupted. Fix: Identify which reaction releases energy and which reaction requires energy.
choices.t: Polymer synthesis decreases because ATP hydrolysis has a net energy cost that takes energy away from synthesis.

stem: A cell synthesizes a polymer from monomers through an energy-requiring reaction coupled to ATP hydrolysis. A treatment disrupts this coupling without affecting the enzymes involved. ATP hydrolysis continues at the same rate, ATP and monomer concentrations remain constant, and no alternative energy-releasing reaction is coupled to polymer synthesis. Which prediction and explanation best describe the immediate effect of the treatment?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: 10 / 0.2 = 50, so the same number of ions in 1/50 of the volume has a 50-fold higher concentration.
choices.t: 50 times higher, because the volume of the lumen is one fiftieth that of the stroma.

choices.r: The number of ions is the same, but the volume is different, and concentration is the number divided by the volume.
choices.t: The same, because the number of ions is the same.

choices.r: This inverts the relationship, because a smaller volume gives a higher concentration.
choices.t: About 50 times lower, because the lumen is smaller.

choices.r: The logarithm of 50 relates to the change in pH units, not to the ratio of concentrations.
choices.t: About 1.7 times higher, which is the logarithm of 50.

stem: In a chloroplast, 3.0 × 10⁵ hydrogen ions are pumped into the thylakoid lumen, which has a volume of 0.2 cubic micrometers. The stroma has a volume of 10 cubic micrometers. Compared with the concentration the same hydrogen ions would have if spread through the stroma, what is the H⁺ concentration in the lumen?
subject: biology

choices.r: The solute molecules inside and outside speed up equally, so they leave and enter at equal rates and there is no net outflow.
choices.t: Net movement of solute out of the cell begins, because faster molecules leave more easily.

choices.r: Both sides are warmed equally, so molecules on neither side gain an advantage and no net inflow results.
choices.t: Net movement of solute into the cell begins, because the molecules outside have more energy.

choices.r: Correct: Higher temperature increases the rate of movement in both directions equally, so equilibrium concentrations are unchanged and no net movement occurs.
choices.t: The concentrations stay equal, but the number of molecules crossing in each direction per minute increases equally.

choices.r: Warming makes membranes more fluid, not less, and it increases rather than stops the exchange.
choices.t: Transport stops, because the membrane becomes less fluid at higher temperatures.

stem: A cell and its surroundings are at equilibrium for a nonmetabolized permeable solute, with equal concentrations inside and out. The temperature of the system is then raised by 10°C, which increases the speed of molecular motion. Which prediction is most reasonable?
subject: biology

choices.r: Heat does not rearrange the order of amino acids, which are joined by strong covalent peptide bonds.
choices.t: The student is correct, because heat rearranges amino acids in the polypeptide.

choices.r: Heat does not convert protein into fat, since the chemical composition of a protein stays amino acid based.
choices.t: The student is correct, because heat converts the protein into fat.

choices.r: Correct: Cooking denatures albumin by disrupting weak interactions; exposed hydrophobic regions cause aggregation, and the primary structure stays unchanged.
choices.t: The student is incorrect, because heat unfolds the protein and exposes hydrophobic regions, which lets the chains stick together and form a solid, while the sequence stays the same.

choices.r: The egg white changes visibly at cooking temperatures, which shows that proteins are affected.
choices.t: The student is incorrect, because heat has no effect on proteins at cooking temperatures.

stem: A student boils an egg. The clear liquid egg white, which is mostly the protein albumin dissolved in water, becomes an opaque white solid. The student claims the heat must have changed the protein's amino acid sequence. Which response is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, so they would not take up the heavy nitrogen label even though they store energy.
choices.t: Triglycerides and DNA, because both store energy and information in long chains.

choices.r: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose containing no nitrogen, so structural function does not determine nitrogen content.
choices.t: Cellulose and proteins, because both are structural polymers.

choices.r: Carbohydrates and triglycerides contain no nitrogen, so not every molecule would be heavier.
choices.t: All four molecules, because every biological molecule contains nitrogen.

choices.r: Correct: Nitrogen is in the amino group of amino acids and in the bases of nucleotides, but triglycerides and cellulose contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
choices.t: Proteins and DNA, because amino acids and nucleotide bases contain nitrogen, whereas triglycerides and cellulose do not.

stem: Algae are grown for several generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source is a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N). The cells are then broken open and the following molecules are purified and compared with those from algae grown in normal nitrogen: triglycerides, cellulose, proteins, and DNA. Which purified molecules are expected to be heavier than normal?
subject: biology

choices.r: At 600 mOsm/L the cells would shrink, not stay normal, and at 280 mOsm/L, which is isotonic, they would not shrink.
choices.t: P = 600 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L

choices.r: At 50 mOsm/L the cells would swell and lyse, not remain normal, and 600 mOsm/L would shrink them rather than burst them.
choices.t: P = 50 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L

choices.r: P is isotonic so no net water movement; Q is hypertonic so water leaves and the cells shrink; R is hypotonic so water enters and cells swell and lyse.
choices.t: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 600 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L

choices.r: Q and R are reversed: a 50 mOsm/L solution is hypotonic and would cause swelling, while 600 mOsm/L would cause shrinking.
choices.t: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 50 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L

stem: Animal cells without a cell wall, whose cytoplasm has an osmolarity of about 280 mOsm/L, were placed in three unlabeled solutions for 10 minutes. In Solution P, the cells kept their normal shape. In Solution Q, the cells shrank and their surfaces became wrinkled. In Solution R, the cells swelled and about half burst. Which set of osmolarities is most consistent with the outcomes for P, Q, and R respectively?
subject: biology

choices.r: Polysaccharides are polymers of monosaccharides, and nucleotides come from nucleic acids.
choices.t: The polysaccharide releases nucleotides.

choices.r: Polypeptides break down to amino acids, and glycerol and fatty acids come from triglycerides.
choices.t: The polypeptide releases glycerol and fatty acids.

choices.r: Correct: A nucleic acid is a polymer of nucleotides, so hydrolysis of a DNA strand releases nucleotides.
choices.t: The DNA strand releases nucleotides.

choices.r: Triglycerides break down to glycerol and fatty acids, and amino acids come from the hydrolysis of proteins.
choices.t: The triglyceride releases amino acids.

stem: A cell extract contains a polysaccharide, a polypeptide, a DNA strand, and a triglyceride. Complete hydrolysis of each releases its building blocks. Which pairing of molecule and the products of its hydrolysis is correct?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: a difference of 0.8 units from single tubes could be within normal variation, and replicates allow the difference to be judged against the spread.
choices.t: Run several replicate tubes at each temperature and compare the means and the spread of the replicates.

choices.r: Changing the 35°C condition to 38°C does not address whether the original difference was real, and it changes the variable under test.
choices.t: Increase the temperature difference to 3°C by repeating the 35°C tube at 38°C.

choices.r: Dropping the 30°C tube removes the comparison that the claim depends on.
choices.t: Use only the 35°C tube, since it had the higher rate.

choices.r: Raising substrate only in one tube adds a second variable and makes the comparison invalid.
choices.t: Switch to a higher substrate concentration in the 35°C tube only.

stem: A student measures the rate of an enzyme at 30°C and at 35°C using one tube at each temperature. The rates are 12.0 and 12.8 units. She concludes that the enzyme is more active at 35°C. Which change would best strengthen the conclusion?
subject: biology

choices.r: The detergent used does not cut peptide bonds, so a single 120 kDa chain would give a 120 kDa band.
choices.t: One polypeptide of 120 kDa, because the detergent cut it into pieces.

choices.r: If all four were linked by disulfide bonds, the band without reducing agent would be 120 kDa.
choices.t: Four identical 30 kDa polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds into a single unit.

choices.r: Correct: The 60 kDa bands show two pairs linked by covalent disulfide bonds, and the 30 kDa band after reduction shows each pair is two 30 kDa chains, giving four chains.
choices.t: Four 30 kDa polypeptides, in which pairs are joined by disulfide bonds and the two pairs are held together by noncovalent interactions.

choices.r: Only one band size appears under each condition, so the sample does not contain a second type of polypeptide.
choices.t: Two different polypeptides of 60 kDa and 30 kDa that are held together by noncovalent interactions.

stem: A protein has a mass of 120 kDa in its native form. On a gel containing a detergent that separates subunits held by noncovalent interactions and unfolds each chain but does not break covalent bonds, the protein gives a single band at 60 kDa. When a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds is also added, the protein gives a single band at 30 kDa. Which structure is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: In this pathway growth factor acts by phosphorylating Rb, and without Rb that step is not needed.
choices.t: S-phase genes stay off until growth factor is added, because E2F also needs the growth factor.

choices.r: Rb binds E2F and does not make it, so losing Rb frees E2F and does not remove it.
choices.t: S-phase genes are off in these cells, because Rb is needed to make E2F.

choices.r: The stem places Rb's role at the control of S-phase genes in G1, and not at G2.
choices.t: The cells arrest in G2, because Rb acts only at the G2 checkpoint.

choices.r: Correct: Rb normally holds E2F inactive; without Rb, E2F is released regardless of growth factor, so S-phase genes can be turned on and cells can pass the G1 checkpoint.
choices.t: E2F is free and S-phase genes are expressed, so the cells can enter S phase without growth factor.

stem: The Rb protein binds the transcription factor E2F in G1 and prevents E2F from turning on S-phase genes. Growth factor signaling leads to phosphorylation of Rb, which releases E2F. A cell line has no functional Rb. The cells are grown without growth factor. Which result is predicted?
subject: biology

choices.r: Feedback means the output influences its own production, and ethylene production is controlled by ethylene, so feedback is present.
choices.t: The claim is correct, because ethylene production keeps changing and so there is no feedback.

choices.r: Positive feedback loops are feedback too, and they amplify a change.
choices.t: The claim is correct, because only negative feedback loops count as feedback.

choices.r: No set point is being defended, and the ethylene level keeps rising instead of returning to a value.
choices.t: The claim is wrong, because this is negative feedback with a set point at a very high ethylene level.

choices.r: Correct: ethylene stimulates more ethylene, so the output amplifies the change; keeping a variable near a set point describes negative feedback only.
choices.t: The claim is wrong: this is a positive feedback loop, in which the output increases the stimulus and drives the variable further from its starting value.

stem: A ripening apple releases ethylene gas. Ethylene triggers cells in the apple, and in nearby apples, to make more ethylene, so the ethylene concentration rises rapidly. A student claims: "A feedback loop must keep a variable steady, so this cannot be a feedback loop at all." Which evaluation is best?
subject: biology

choices.r: Peptide bonds form only between the amino group and carboxyl group of amino acids during translation; R groups do not form them with other proteins.
choices.t: The leucine side chains form peptide bonds with neighboring enzyme molecules, joining the proteins into one large covalent polymer.

choices.r: Hydrophobic side chains exposed on the surface cluster together away from water, so separate protein molecules stick together.
choices.t: The exposed nonpolar leucine side chains on separate molecules associate with each other to avoid water, linking the molecules through hydrophobic interactions.

choices.r: Nonpolar side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; serine, the polar residue that was replaced, could.
choices.t: The leucine side chains form strong hydrogen bonds with water, which pulls the molecules together into aggregates.

choices.r: Leucine's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged, so it contributes no charge and no ionic attraction.
choices.t: The leucine substitution adds a negative charge, so the neighboring molecules are attracted to each other by ionic bonds.

stem: A mutation in a bacterial enzyme replaces a serine (polar, uncharged) on the protein's surface with leucine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). The mutant enzyme folds normally and remains active, but in water its molecules clump together into large aggregates, whereas the normal enzyme stays dispersed. Which best explains why the mutant molecules aggregate?
subject: biology

choices.r: The triglyceride floats on top, which shows it is less dense than water, so mass is not the cause.
choices.t: The triglyceride has a larger mass than the phospholipid, so it sinks.

choices.r: A triglyceride has three fatty acid tails and a phospholipid has two, so the triglyceride does not have fewer.
choices.t: The triglyceride has fewer fatty acid tails than the phospholipid, so it cannot form droplets.

choices.r: If the triglyceride were hydrophilic it would dissolve, but the observed layer of merged droplets shows it is hydrophobic.
choices.t: The triglyceride is hydrophilic, so it dissolves completely in water.

choices.r: Correct: A triglyceride is entirely nonpolar, so it separates from water as a layer, but a phospholipid is amphipathic and its polar head faces water while tails face each other.
choices.t: The triglyceride has no polar head group, so the whole molecule is nonpolar and is excluded from water, whereas the phospholipid has a polar phosphate-containing head and nonpolar tails.

stem: Equal amounts of three lipids are added to separate tubes of water and shaken. Phospholipid: forms a cloudy mixture of tiny sacs, each enclosing a droplet of water. Triglyceride: forms oily droplets that merge into a layer on top and shows no ordered structure. Which statement best explains why the triglyceride does not assemble like the phospholipid?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Mitochondrial ribosomes share the drug sensitivity of bacterial ribosomes but not of the cell's cytosolic ribosomes, supporting a bacterial origin for mitochondria.
choices.t: Mitochondrial ribosomes are similar to bacterial ribosomes, which is consistent with a bacterial ancestor.

choices.r: Where mitochondria are made does not explain why their ribosomes are drug sensitive, and a nuclear origin would predict the same behavior as cytosolic ribosomes.
choices.t: Mitochondria are made in the nucleus, which is why they respond to the antibiotic.

choices.r: The experiment measures protein synthesis in mitochondria and shows that they carry it out, because it is blocked by the drug.
choices.t: Mitochondria do not carry out protein synthesis, so the observed change must be due to ATP depletion.

choices.r: The cytosolic ribosomes are unaffected, which shows they differ from bacterial ribosomes rather than resembling them.
choices.t: Cytosolic ribosomes of the rat cells are bacterial in origin, since they are unaffected.

stem: The antibiotic chloramphenicol blocks protein synthesis by bacterial ribosomes but does not block protein synthesis by the cytosolic ribosomes of eukaryotic cells. When added to isolated mitochondria from rat liver, it stops mitochondrial protein synthesis, while protein synthesis in the cytosol of the same cells is unaffected. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Ribosomes make enzymes independent of the Golgi complex, and the drug is stated not to affect synthesis.
choices.t: The enzymes are no longer made, because the Golgi complex supplies the ribosomes that carry out their synthesis.

choices.r: The Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins; it does not digest them or speed up breakdown of cell components.
choices.t: The enzymes are digested by the Golgi complex, so worn-out components are broken down faster than in untreated cells.

choices.r: Lysosomal enzymes are made at the rough ER; the lysosome receives them and does not make them.
choices.t: The enzymes are made inside the lysosomes instead, so worn-out components are digested at the normal rate.

choices.r: Packaging in the Golgi complex is required to deliver enzymes to lysosomes, so digestion falls and material accumulates.
choices.t: The enzymes are still made, but they do not reach lysosomes, so worn-out cell components are digested less and accumulate.

stem: Hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, then modified and sorted in the Golgi complex into vesicles that become lysosomes. A drug prevents the Golgi complex from packaging these enzymes into vesicles but does not affect enzyme synthesis. Which outcome is most likely in the treated cells?
subject: biology

choices.r: The final internal concentration is 10 mM, equal to the outside, so the channel does not cause accumulation.
choices.t: The channel allows the bacteria to accumulate glycerol at a concentration higher than the outside concentration.

choices.r: Correct: The ratio of initial rates is 8 divided by 0.2 = 40, and both end at 10 mM, equal to the outside concentration, so the channel changes the speed but not the equilibrium.
choices.t: The channel increases the initial rate of uptake 40-fold, but does not change the final concentration.

choices.r: The initial rate ratio is 40, not 4, so this understates the effect of the channel on rate.
choices.t: The channel protein increases the initial rate of uptake 4-fold, but does not change the final concentration.

choices.r: Slow uptake in the mutant is consistent with glycerol slowly crossing the bilayer by diffusion, and its final concentration is equal to the outside level, not above it.
choices.t: The mutant bacteria must be using active transport, because uptake still occurs without the channel.

stem: Bacteria with a glycerol channel protein and mutant bacteria lacking it are placed in 10 mM glycerol (which they do not metabolize). The initial rate of uptake is 8 mM per minute in normal bacteria and 0.2 mM per minute in the mutant. After 60 minutes both have 10 mM glycerol inside. Which statement is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: only tube 1 loses blue color; without light, with denatured chloroplasts, or with electron flow blocked, absorbance stays near 0.80.
choices.t: DCPIP is reduced by electrons from light-driven electron transport in intact thylakoids, which needs light, intact membranes and working photosystem II.

choices.r: No CO₂ was supplied or measured, and DCPIP reduction reports electron flow in the light reactions and not carbon fixation.
choices.t: The fall in absorbance in tube 1 shows that the Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ in the light.

choices.r: The changes in tubes 2 to 4 (0.02, 0.01, 0.03) are very small and consistent with no reduction, so light is required.
choices.t: DCPIP is reduced slightly in tubes 2 to 4 and more in tube 1, so light is helpful but not required.

choices.r: Tube 3 contains light but its absorbance barely changes, which shows light alone does not reduce DCPIP.
choices.t: Tube 3 shows that light alone is enough to reduce DCPIP, even in the absence of functional chloroplasts.

stem:
Isolated chloroplast suspensions are mixed with DCPIP, a blue dye that becomes colorless when it accepts electrons. Absorbance (higher means bluer, more unreduced DCPIP) is measured at the start (0.80 in every tube) and after 10 minutes.
Tube | Treatment | Absorbance at 10 min
1 | Intact chloroplasts, light | 0.25
2 | Intact chloroplasts, dark | 0.78
3 | Boiled chloroplasts, light | 0.79
4 | Intact chloroplasts, light, plus DCMU (blocks electron flow from photosystem II) | 0.77
Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Paracrine signaling needs a different nearby cell to receive the signal, and each well has only one cell.
choices.t: Paracrine signaling, because G acts on nearby cells.

choices.r: Correct: each well holds only one cell, so the signal can only come from the cell itself and act on the same cell's receptor; blocking either G or its receptor stops division.
choices.t: Autocrine signaling, because the cell makes a signal that binds its own receptors.

choices.r: There is no neighboring cell to touch, since each cell is alone in its well.
choices.t: Contact-dependent signaling, because G is attached to the membrane of the neighboring cell.

choices.r: Endocrine signaling involves a distant target cell reached by the bloodstream, and no such cell exists in a culture well.
choices.t: Endocrine signaling, because G is carried through fluid to target cells.

stem: A tumor cell line makes growth factor G and has receptors for it. Single cells plated one per well, far from any other cell, still divide in medium with no added growth factor. Adding an antibody that binds and neutralizes G to the medium stops their division, and so does an antibody that blocks the G receptor. Which best classifies the signaling that drives division in these cells?
subject: biology

choices.r: Only a competitive inhibitor is overcome by excess substrate, and this data shows a constant fractional reduction.
choices.t: It will succeed, because every inhibitor loses its effect once substrate is added in large excess.

choices.r: Correct: the inhibited rate is about 50 percent of the uninhibited rate at every concentration (17/33, 25/50, 36/71, 45/91, 49/98), so substrate cannot overcome it, as expected for a noncompetitive inhibitor.
choices.t: It will fail: the rate with inhibitor stays near half of the uninhibited rate at every substrate concentration, which fits an inhibitor that binds outside the active site and lowers the maximum rate.

choices.r: The uninhibited curve also levels off at high substrate because the enzyme is saturated, not denatured.
choices.t: It will fail only because the enzyme is denatured at high substrate concentration, which is why the rate stops rising.

choices.r: The ratio of inhibited to uninhibited rate does not rise with substrate, so the inhibitor is not weaker at higher substrate.
choices.t: It will succeed, because the rates at 2 mM and 4 mM show the inhibitor is weaker at higher substrate.

stem:
A second inhibitor is tested on the same enzyme under identical conditions. Initial rates (relative units per minute) are:
Substrate (mM) | No inhibitor | With inhibitor
2 | 33 | 17
4 | 50 | 25
10 | 71 | 36
40 | 91 | 45
200 | 98 | 49
A student proposes raising the substrate from 40 mM to 200 mM to restore the uninhibited rate. Which statement best evaluates the proposal?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: only the combination of ATP and NADPH restores sugar synthesis in the dark, so both are required, and light acts indirectly through the light reactions.
choices.t: The carbon-fixing reactions do not need light directly, but they need both ATP and NADPH, which the light reactions normally supply.

choices.r: The experiment was done entirely in the dark, and sugar formed when ATP and NADPH were added.
choices.t: The carbon-fixing reactions need light directly, because sugar forms only when the stroma is illuminated.

choices.r: ATP alone raised the label from 1 to 2, which is negligible compared with the 60 seen with both.
choices.t: ATP alone is enough to drive sugar synthesis, since both additions raise the label slightly.

choices.r: NADPH alone gave the same negligible increase, so it cannot drive synthesis without ATP.
choices.t: NADPH alone is enough to drive sugar synthesis because it is the reducing agent.

stem:
Isolated chloroplast stroma (with the Calvin cycle enzymes but no thylakoids) is incubated in the dark with ¹⁴CO₂. The amount of radioactive carbon incorporated into sugar after 10 minutes is:
Additions | ¹⁴C in sugar
None | 1
ATP only | 2
NADPH only | 2
ATP and NADPH | 60
Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Each step only multiplies the number it receives, so fewer K3 means fewer phosphorylated factors.
choices.t: 40,000, unchanged, because the later step adds 10 for each K3 and so corrects the loss.

choices.r: Only one step changed and it was halved from 10 to 5, so the output halves and does not fall to a quarter.
choices.t: 10,000, one fourth of normal, because the change at the second step affects two steps.

choices.r: 40 × 5 = 200 ignores the multiplication by the other steps of the cascade.
choices.t: 200, because only the 5 K3 per K2 matter for the final amount.

choices.r: Correct: normal is 40 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 40,000; with the drug it is 40 × 10 × 5 × 10 = 20,000, which is half.
choices.t: 20,000, half of the normal 40,000, because halving the output of one step halves the final output.

stem: In a kinase cascade, each active kinase K1 activates 10 molecules of K2, each active K2 activates 10 molecules of K3, and each active K3 phosphorylates 10 molecules of a transcription factor. A drug changes K2 so that each active K2 activates only 5 K3 molecules. If 40 K1 molecules are active, which statement describes the number of phosphorylated transcription factor molecules?
subject: biology

choices.r: Boiled saliva is a negative control because its enzyme is denatured and no starch breakdown is expected.
choices.t: Starch solution with boiled saliva, then iodine.

choices.r: Starch with water is a negative control that shows what no breakdown looks like.
choices.t: Starch solution with water instead of saliva, then iodine.

choices.r: There is no starch in this tube, so no breakdown is possible and the tube does not test the assay's ability to detect it.
choices.t: Water with saliva, with no starch, then iodine.

choices.r: Correct: a positive control uses a treatment known to produce the effect; active amylase with starch should lose the blue-black color if the assay works.
choices.t: Starch solution with a commercial amylase solution known to be active, then iodine.

stem: A student uses the iodine test, which turns blue-black with starch, to detect amylase activity in saliva. Before testing saliva she wants to confirm that her assay can detect starch breakdown at all. Which tube is the best positive control?
subject: biology

choices.r: The active site is normal, so the enzyme is not less active, and only the inhibition by Z is gone.
choices.t: Z levels are lower in the mutant, because the mutant enzyme has lost activity.

choices.r: The stem gives no mechanism that removes extra Z, and without feedback the pathway keeps running.
choices.t: Z levels are the same, because the cell breaks down any extra Z.

choices.r: Losing negative feedback does not turn it into positive feedback, and the result is overproduction and not underproduction.
choices.t: Z levels are lower in the mutant, because the loss of feedback inhibition acts as positive feedback.

choices.r: Correct: the active site works but the allosteric inhibition is lost, so enzyme 1 keeps making product however much Z is present, and Z accumulates.
choices.t: Z levels are higher in the mutant, because enzyme 1 stays active when Z accumulates.

stem: In a bacterium, enzyme 1 begins a pathway that makes end product Z. Z normally binds an allosteric site on enzyme 1 and inhibits it. A mutant enzyme 1 has a normal active site but can no longer bind Z. Compared with the normal bacterium, which result is expected?
subject: biology

choices.r: The sequence is the same after heating, so peptide bonds were not broken.
choices.t: Heating broke peptide bonds, which changed the amino acid sequence.

choices.r: Correct: Unchanged sequence and mass show that peptide bonds were not broken, while loss of helices and activity shows the folded structure was disrupted.
choices.t: Heating disrupted hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that maintain secondary and tertiary structure, but left the covalent peptide bonds and primary structure intact.

choices.r: Heating a purified protein does not change genes or make a new protein, and no DNA is present in the sample.
choices.t: Heating changed the gene that codes for the enzyme, so a new protein was made.

choices.r: The unchanged molecular mass shows that no amino acids were removed.
choices.t: Heating removed amino acids from the chain, which lowered the helix content.

stem: An enzyme is heated to 95°C for 5 minutes and cooled to 25°C. Before heating, the enzyme is active, the amino acid sequence is determined, and a measurement finds that 40% of the chain is in alpha helices. After heating and cooling, activity is zero, the amino acid sequence is unchanged, the molecular mass is unchanged, and helices account for 5% of the chain. Which statement best explains the results?
subject: biology

choices.r: Equal volume does not mean equal surface area, because surface area depends on how the volume is divided.
choices.t: The total surface area is the same, because the total volume is the same.

choices.r: Correct: Total volume is 216 for both (6³ and 27 × 2³). Surface area for Arrangement 1 is 6 × 36 = 216; for Arrangement 2 it is 27 × 24 = 648, which is three times as large.
choices.t: The total surface area of Arrangement 2 is three times that of Arrangement 1, because each small cell has a surface-area-to-volume ratio of 3 and the large cell has a ratio of 1.

choices.r: Each small cell does have less surface area (24 versus 216), but there are 27 of them, so the total is larger, not smaller.
choices.t: The total surface area of Arrangement 2 is one third that of Arrangement 1, because each small cell has far less surface area than the large cell.

choices.r: Multiplying by the number of cells ignores that each small cell has much less surface area than the large cell (24 compared with 216).
choices.t: The total surface area of Arrangement 2 is 27 times that of Arrangement 1, because there are 27 cells.

stem: A researcher compares two hypothetical arrangements of the same total volume of cytoplasm. Arrangement 1 is one cube-shaped cell with an edge of 6 micrometers. Arrangement 2 is 27 cube-shaped cells, each with an edge of 2 micrometers. Which statement correctly compares the total surface area available for exchange with the environment?
subject: biology

choices.r: Tempting because 75 minus 40 is 35 and it looks like a donated amount. But enzymes do not add energy; they provide an easier path. Fix: describe the enzyme as lowering the barrier from 75 to 40 kJ/mol, never as adding energy.
choices.t: It supplies 35 kJ/mol of energy to the substrate so the reaction can start and then the substrate has enough energy to react without help.

choices.r: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy, not by changing the reactants' or products' energy. The reaction therefore reaches the same overall 30 kJ/mol release, only faster.
choices.t: It lowers the energy barrier to 40 kJ/mol, and the reaction still releases 30 kJ/mol overall.

choices.r: Tempting if you add the barrier reduction to the energy released. But the overall energy change depends only on reactants and products. Fix: keep the energy released (30 kJ/mol) separate from the activation energy, the only value the enzyme changes.
choices.t: It makes the reaction release 65 kJ/mol overall, because the barrier is 35 kJ/mol lower.

choices.r: Tempting because the enzyme binds the substrate. But the enzyme is released unchanged after catalysis and can be reused. Fix: describe enzyme binding as temporary, with the enzyme unchanged and reusable after the reaction.
choices.t: It is used up in the reaction as it permanently joins the substrate.

stem: An uncatalyzed reaction has an activation energy of 75 kJ/mol and releases 30 kJ/mol overall. An enzyme lowers the activation energy to 40 kJ/mol. What does the enzyme change?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Loss of microtubules leaves shape and attachment largely intact, but vesicle distribution and chromosome separation fail, which are the two microtubule functions of transport tracks and spindle.
choices.t: Microtubules serve as tracks for motor proteins that move vesicles, and they form the spindle that separates chromosomes.

choices.r: Mechanical strength comes mainly from intermediate filaments, and the cells here keep their shape without microtubules.
choices.t: Microtubules supply the main mechanical strength that keeps the cell from tearing under stress.

choices.r: The contractile ring is made of actin filaments, and the observed failure is in chromosome separation rather than pinching.
choices.t: Microtubules form the contractile ring that pinches the dividing cell in two.

choices.r: Ribosomes assemble polypeptides using mRNA and are not built on microtubules.
choices.t: Microtubules are the structures on which ribosomes assemble polypeptides.

stem: A drug disassembles microtubules in cultured fibroblasts but does not affect actin filaments or intermediate filaments. After treatment, researchers observe that (1) the cells stay attached to the dish and keep most of their shape, (2) membrane-bound vesicles accumulate near the center of the cell rather than being distributed through it, and (3) in cells that begin to divide, the chromosomes do not separate into two groups. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Hydrolysis adds water, so the products include the mass of the added water and the monomers together weigh more than the polymer.
choices.t: 3000 g/mol, because mass is conserved and the monomers have the same mass as the polymer.

choices.r: Correct: A chain of 24 monomers has 23 bonds, so hydrolysis adds 23 x 18 = 414 g/mol of water: 3000 + 414 = 3414 g/mol.
choices.t: 3414 g/mol, because 23 water molecules are added.

choices.r: This subtracts the water mass, but hydrolysis adds water rather than removing it.
choices.t: 2586 g/mol, because the monomers are smaller than the polymer.

choices.r: This uses 24 bonds, but a linear chain of 24 monomers has only 23 bonds.
choices.t: 3432 g/mol, because 24 water molecules are added.

stem: A linear polymer with a molar mass of 3000 g/mol contains 24 monomers. Complete hydrolysis converts it into 24 free monomers by adding water at every bond (18 g/mol per water). What is the total molar mass of the 24 free monomers?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: starved cells hold only 3.0 pg, so they are in G1 or G0; after serum, many cells hold intermediate or 6.0 pg amounts, which means DNA replication occurred.
choices.t: The starved cells were arrested before DNA replication (in G1 or G0), and serum let them re-enter the cycle, replicate DNA and move on.

choices.r: Cells arrested in G2 would hold 6.0 pg, and the starved cells held 3.0 pg.
choices.t: The starved cells were arrested in G2, and serum made them divide and enter G1.

choices.r: Cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg are copying their DNA, which shows replication happened and was not blocked.
choices.t: Serum blocks DNA replication, so the cells between 3.0 and 6.0 pg are damaged.

choices.r: Cells that skip S would not gain DNA, and many cells now have more than 3.0 pg.
choices.t: Serum makes cells skip S phase and go directly into mitosis.

stem: Cells are kept in medium without serum for 4 days. Flow cytometry shows 93% of the cells at 3.0 pg of DNA (the amount in G1 before replication). Twenty hours after serum is added, 40% of the cells are at 3.0 pg, 35% are between 3.0 and 6.0 pg, and 25% are at 6.0 pg. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: even at 50 mM substrate the rate at 55°C is only 3 compared with 40 at 25°C, so the limit is the amount of functional enzyme and not the substrate supply.
choices.t: It will not help much: at 55°C the maximum rate is lowered because much of the enzyme has lost its active-site shape, and more substrate cannot restore the lost enzyme.

choices.r: Raising substrate helps only if substrate is limiting, and the rate at 55°C stays low even at 50 mM, which shows the enzyme is the limit.
choices.t: It will fully restore activity, because substrate concentration alone limits every enzyme.

choices.r: Substrate does not cause a denatured protein to refold, and the data show no recovery.
choices.t: It will help because higher substrate concentrations make the active site refold.

choices.r: The rate rises from 1 to 3 with more substrate, so some functional enzyme still binds substrate, and the issue is that most of it is lost.
choices.t: It will not help, because substrate cannot bind a heated enzyme at all.

stem:
An enzyme is assayed at two temperatures and two substrate concentrations. Enzyme amount and pH are identical.
Temperature | 1 mM substrate | 50 mM substrate
25°C | 10 | 40
55°C | 1 | 3
A student proposes to rescue the activity at 55°C by adding more substrate. Which evaluation is best?
subject: biology

choices.r: The analog binds the pump yet produces no transport, so binding by itself is not the energy source.
choices.t: Binding of a nucleotide to the pump supplies the energy for transport.

choices.r: Correct: the analog binds but is not hydrolyzed and gives no transport, so the energy for transport comes from the hydrolysis step.
choices.t: Transport needs the energy released when the terminal phosphate bond of ATP is hydrolyzed, and not only the binding of a nucleotide.

choices.r: The stem says the analog binds the pump like ATP, and nothing suggests denaturation, so the lack of hydrolysis is the key difference.
choices.t: AMP-PNP denatures the pump before transport can occur.

choices.r: ATP is a substrate and energy carrier, and the pump is the enzyme, so ATP does not act as an enzyme here.
choices.t: ATP acts as an enzyme that lowers the activation energy for calcium movement.

stem: Vesicles containing a calcium pump are placed in a solution with calcium. With ATP, calcium accumulates inside the vesicles. With AMP-PNP, an analog that binds the pump like ATP but cannot be hydrolyzed, no calcium accumulates. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: the human enzyme peaks near 37°C and the hot-spring enzyme near 80°C; below the optimum low rates reflect low kinetic energy, above it they reflect loss of active-site shape.
choices.t: Each rate rises with temperature up to the enzyme's optimum and then falls as heat disrupts the active site, and the hot-spring enzyme's optimum is much higher than the human enzyme's.

choices.r: Cool temperatures slow molecular motion and collisions but do not denature a protein, so the low rate at 20°C does not indicate denaturation.
choices.t: The hot-spring enzyme is denatured at 20°C and 37°C, which is why its rates there are low.

choices.r: The stem holds the substrate concentration the same, and the decline at high temperature comes from loss of the active-site shape.
choices.t: The human enzyme's rate falls above 37°C because the substrate is used up at higher temperatures.

choices.r: The human enzyme has higher rates at 20°C and 37°C (6 and 20 versus 1 and 3), so the claim of a higher rate at every temperature is false.
choices.t: The hot-spring enzyme has a higher rate at every temperature tested because it comes from an extremophile.

stem:
A researcher measures the initial rate of a similar reaction catalyzed by an enzyme from a human cell and an enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium. Substrate concentration and pH are identical in all tests.
Temperature (°C) | Human enzyme rate | Hot-spring enzyme rate
20 | 6 | 1
37 | 20 | 3
60 | 2 | 12
80 | 0 | 20
95 | 0 | 4
Which statement is best supported by the data?
subject: biology

choices.r: If mitosis were faster, fewer cells would be caught in mitosis at a moment, and metaphase would not hold most of them.
choices.t: The drug speeds up mitosis, because far more cells are in mitosis after treatment.

choices.r: Correct: metaphase cells rise from 3 to 118 while anaphase and telophase stay near 1 to 3, so cells reach metaphase and cannot go on.
choices.t: The drug blocks the move from metaphase to anaphase, so cells that enter mitosis pile up in metaphase.

choices.r: Interphase cells fell because cells entered mitosis and stayed in it, so entry is not blocked.
choices.t: The drug stops cells from entering mitosis, because the number of interphase cells fell.

choices.r: Telophase cells did not accumulate (3 cells), so the block comes before telophase.
choices.t: The drug blocks cytokinesis, because cells accumulate at the end of mitosis.

stem:
A researcher counts 200 cells from a culture before and after 6 hours of treatment with a drug.
Phase | Before drug | After 6 hours of drug
Interphase | 190 | 70
Prophase | 4 | 8
Metaphase | 3 | 118
Anaphase | 1 | 1
Telophase | 2 | 3
Which interpretation is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Specific heat concerns temperature change within a phase and does not cause beading on a hydrophobic surface.
choices.t: High specific heat explains both phenomena: it slows temperature change and causes water to resist spreading on surfaces.

choices.r: Adhesion helps condensation on hydrophilic bumps, but weak adhesion to hydrophobic material does not explain the water-to-water attraction that maintains beads.
choices.t: Adhesion explains both: water clings to hydrophilic bumps and rolls along hydrophobic troughs because it adheres strongly to both surfaces.

choices.r: Vaporization requires substantial energy, and hydrophobic interactions are not a simple electrostatic repulsion of water molecules.
choices.t: Polarity alone explains both: polar water requires no energy to vaporize and is repelled by every nonpolar surface.

choices.r: Hydrogen bonding produces a high heat of vaporization and strong cohesion. Cohesion exceeds adhesion to a hydrophobic surface, maintaining droplets that can roll.
choices.t: High heat of vaporization means each gram that evaporates absorbs substantial energy; cohesion keeps water molecules attracted to one another so they bead on hydrophobic surfaces.

stem: Which property of water explains the large energy transfer associated with evaporation, and which property explains why liquid water beads and rolls along hydrophobic troughs rather than spreading flat?
stimulus: Namib Desert beetles collect water by tilting toward coastal fog at dawn. Droplets condense on hydrophilic bumps on their back surfaces and roll toward their mouths along hydrophobic troughs. Researchers noted that beetles must collect water before peak daytime heat causes significant evaporative loss from their body surface. A separate study found that transferring the same mass of water from liquid to vapor requires substantially more energy than melting the same mass of ice.
subject: biology

choices.r: Label appears in the rough ER at 2 minutes, which shows the hormone was synthesized, so translation was not blocked.
choices.t: Translation of the hormone on ribosomes, because the hormone cannot be made without it.

choices.r: A block at the plasma membrane would let label build up in secretory vesicles, but none is seen beyond the rough ER.
choices.t: Fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane, which releases the protein from the cell.

choices.r: A Golgi modification block would leave label piled up in the Golgi complex, yet no label ever reaches it.
choices.t: Modification of the protein inside the Golgi complex, which prepares it for release.

choices.r: Correct: Label does enter the rough ER at 2 minutes, so the protein is made and enters the ER; it never reaches the Golgi complex, so the first step that fails is ER-to-Golgi vesicle transport.
choices.t: Budding or transport of vesicles that carry the protein from the rough ER to the Golgi complex.

stem: Cells that secrete a protein hormone are given a brief pulse of radioactive amino acids and then transferred to nonradioactive medium. In normal cells the label appears in the rough ER after 2 minutes, in the Golgi complex after 15 minutes, in vesicles near the plasma membrane after 30 minutes, and outside the cell after 60 minutes. In cells treated with drug X, label is present in the rough ER at 2 minutes and is still found only in the rough ER at 15, 30, and 60 minutes, with none detected in the Golgi complex or outside the cell. Which step does drug X most likely block?
subject: biology

choices.t: The membrane lipid is a phospholipid with a phosphate-containing head group, often with a nitrogen-containing group, whereas a triglyceride has only glycerol and fatty acids.

choices.r: A membrane lipid does not contain amino acids or peptide bonds, and its nitrogen comes from a small head group.
choices.t: The membrane lipid contains amino acids, which a seed fat lacks.

stem: A lipid extract from a cell membrane is analyzed and found to contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and a small amount of nitrogen. A fat extract from a seed contains only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Which statement best explains the difference between the two extracts?
subject: biology

choices.t: Add 2 mL of the untreated extract to the same hydrogen peroxide solution.

choices.r: Changing the peroxide concentration tests a substrate effect and does not distinguish an enzyme from other components of the extract.
choices.t: Add 1 mL of the untreated extract to a hydrogen peroxide solution at a lower concentration.

stem: A student grinds potato tissue and filters the liquid. When she adds 1 mL of the extract to hydrogen peroxide, bubbles form quickly. She claims that an enzyme in the extract causes the bubbling. Which additional treatment would best test whether the bubbling depends on the enzyme's native, folded structure rather than on some other component of the extract?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Both cell types end at 5.0 mM, which equals the outside concentration, but W gets there in about 10 minutes and X takes about 360 minutes, so the carrier speeds equilibration without changing where it ends.
choices.t: The carrier increases the rate at which the sugar reaches equilibrium but does not change the final concentration, which is 5.0 mM in both cell types.

choices.r: The internal concentration of W stops at 5.0 mM, equal to the outside concentration, so there is no concentration above it.
choices.t: The carrier in cell type W concentrates the sugar inside the cell above the outside concentration.

choices.r: Active transport would cause accumulation above the outside concentration, but X stops at 5.0 mM and is slow because the sugar crosses the bilayer poorly.
choices.t: Cell type X uses active transport, because its internal concentration reaches 5.0 mM only after a long time.

choices.r: Facilitated diffusion does not require ATP, and X still takes up sugar slowly without it.
choices.t: The carrier requires ATP, which cell type X lacks, so uptake is slow in cell type X.

stem: Cells are placed in medium containing 5 mM of a nonmetabolized sugar, and internal concentration (mM) is measured. Cell type W, which has a sugar carrier: 0 minutes, 0; 2 minutes, 3.5; 5 minutes, 4.8; 10 minutes, 5.0; 30 minutes, 5.0. Cell type X, which lacks the carrier: 0 minutes, 0; 2 minutes, 0.1; 5 minutes, 0.2; 10 minutes, 0.4; 30 minutes, 1.2; 120 minutes, 3.0; 360 minutes, 5.0. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Melting does not break covalent bonds; water molecules stay as H2O, and only intermolecular hydrogen bonds loosen.
choices.t: The added energy breaks the covalent O-H bonds in water molecules, which stops the temperature from rising.

choices.r: Correct: A temperature plateau during a phase change shows that energy is being absorbed to disrupt intermolecular hydrogen bonds instead of increasing kinetic energy.
choices.t: The added energy is used to break hydrogen bonds in the ice lattice, so it changes the arrangement of molecules rather than raising their average kinetic energy.

choices.r: The heater keeps running, so energy continues to enter the sample, and the flat temperature means that energy is being used for something other than warming.
choices.t: The heater stops transferring energy to the sample while the ice is present.

choices.r: If no energy were needed, the ice would melt instantly and there would be no plateau, but melting does require energy.
choices.t: Ice and liquid water have identical energies, so no energy is needed to melt the ice.

stem: A block of ice at -10°C is heated at a constant rate in an insulated container. The temperature rises steadily to 0°C, then stays at 0°C for several minutes while the heater keeps running, and then rises again once all of the ice has become liquid water. Which statement best explains the flat portion at 0°C?
subject: biology

choices.r: The problem states that Q is an integral membrane protein, and its digestion in leaky cells shows it is exposed on the inner surface.
choices.t: Protein Q is not part of the membrane, because the protease cannot reach it in intact cells.

choices.r: Correct: In intact cells the enzyme can reach only the outer surface, so digestion of P in intact cells places a domain of P outside; Q is digested only when the enzyme enters the cytoplasm, so its accessible region faces the cytoplasm.
choices.t: Protein P has an exposed region on the outer surface of the cell, and the exposed region of protein Q faces the cytoplasm.

choices.r: Digestion from outside shows an exposed outer domain, but both proteins are integral, so this does not make P peripheral.
choices.t: Protein P is a peripheral protein, because the protease can digest it from outside the cell.

choices.r: Q is digested when the enzyme reaches the cytoplasm, which shows an accessible inner domain rather than complete protection.
choices.t: Protein Q is deeper in the hydrophobic core than protein P, so it is protected from the protease on both sides.

stem: A protease that cannot cross the plasma membrane is added to two preparations of red blood cells: intact cells and cells that have been made leaky so the enzyme can reach the cytoplasm. Protein P is digested in both preparations. Protein Q is digested only in the leaky preparation. Both proteins are integral membrane proteins. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: The total number of glucose units is the same, but the enzyme acts on ends, so the rate depends on how many ends are available.
choices.t: About the same, because both polymers contain 10,000 glucose units.

choices.r: Correct: Rate scales with the number of ends: 1,001 ends versus 1 end gives about 1,000 times the initial rate.
choices.t: About 1,000 times faster, because H has about 1,001 ends for the enzyme to act on, compared with 1 end in L.

choices.r: The branch spacing of 10 units is not the ratio of ends, and 10,000 units with a branch every 10 give about 1,000 ends.
choices.t: About 10 times faster, because H has a branch every 10 units.

choices.r: Branching increases the number of ends, so a compact shape does not slow release at each end.
choices.t: About 10 times slower, because branching makes H more compact.

stem: Two storage polymers each contain 10,000 glucose units. Polymer L is unbranched and has one end where glucose is removed. Polymer H has a branch about every 10 glucose units, which gives it about 1,001 chain ends. An enzyme removes glucose only from the ends of chains, one unit at a time, and each end is processed at the same rate. How does the initial rate of glucose release from H compare with that from L?
subject: biology

choices.r: Correct: Oxygen crosses a million times faster than urea, and sodium ion (23 daltons) is far slower than urea (60 daltons), so mass alone fails; the order follows nonpolar, then polar, then charged, with larger polar molecules slower than small polar ones.
choices.t: Both size and chemical character matter: small nonpolar molecules cross fastest, larger polar molecules cross slowly, and a charged ion crosses slowest even though it is smaller than urea.

choices.r: Sodium ion has a smaller mass than urea and oxygen has a similar mass to the ion yet the ion is slower by a factor of about 10 billion, so mass alone does not explain the order.
choices.t: Permeability decreases as molecular mass increases, so mass alone determines how fast a substance crosses.

choices.r: The hydrophobic core of the bilayer repels polar substances and admits nonpolar ones, so polar molecules cross more slowly.
choices.t: Polar molecules cross faster than nonpolar molecules because they dissolve readily in the aqueous solutions on both sides of the membrane.

choices.r: The values differ by a factor of ten billion, which is far too large to be measurement error.
choices.t: The membrane is equally permeable to all four substances, and the differences result from measurement error.

stem: A researcher measures how quickly four substances cross an artificial membrane made only of phospholipids, with no proteins. Relative permeability is reported in arbitrary units. Oxygen (32 daltons, uncharged, nonpolar): 1,000,000. Urea (60 daltons, uncharged, polar): 1,000. Glucose (180 daltons, uncharged, polar): 1. Sodium ion (23 daltons, charged): 0.0001. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
subject: biology

choices.r: The Krebs cycle also depends on NAD⁺ that the electron transport chain regenerates, so it cannot speed up without oxygen.
choices.t: Without oxygen, glycolysis stops and the Krebs cycle runs faster to supply the ATP.

choices.r: The data show about 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically versus 30 aerobically, so the yield per glucose is lower.
choices.t: Fermentation yields more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration, so the cells can use their glucose more freely.

choices.r: Correct: ATP per glucose is 30 aerobically (150/5) and 2 anaerobically (90/45), consistent with fermentation regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue at a low yield.
choices.t: Without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot regenerate NAD⁺, but fermentation does; glycolysis continues at about 2 ATP per glucose, so far more glucose must be used for ATP.

choices.r: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, and mitochondria cannot run the electron transport chain without oxygen, so more glucose in the mitochondria would not raise the yield.
choices.t: Without oxygen more glucose enters the mitochondria, where it is oxidized with a higher yield.

stem:

Which explanation best accounts for the data?
subject: biology

choices.t: About 0.04 hours, because 8 of 200 cells are in metaphase.

choices.t: About 1.9 hours, because 8 of every 100 cells are in metaphase.

choices.t: About 4.8 hours, because 8 of the 40 dividing cells are in metaphase.

choices.t: About 1.0 hour, because 8/200 of the cells are in metaphase and the cycle is 24 hours long.

stem: A researcher examines 200 cells from a growing root tip under the microscope. The cell cycle in this tissue lasts 24 hours. Counts: interphase 160, prophase 16, metaphase 8, anaphase 6, telophase 10. About how long does a cell spend in metaphase?
subject: biology

choices.r: Incorrect. The Glu6Val substitution does not disrupt β-globin's secondary structure -- HbS folds normally into the same alpha-helical/quaternary structure as HbA. Polymerization occurs through an intact fold's surface chemistry, not helix unfolding.
choices.t: Valine's smaller side chain leaves a gap that destabilizes β-globin's alpha-helix, unfolding HbS into fibers

choices.r: Deoxygenation causes a conformational change in HbS that exposes a hydrophobic pocket. Valine's nonpolar side chain associates with this pocket rather than contacting water, promoting chain formation. HbA's glutamic acid at position 6 is charged and cannot insert into this hydrophobic pocket.
choices.t: The hydrophobic valine at position 6 inserts into the complementary hydrophobic pocket exposed on adjacent deoxygenated HbS molecules, driving chain polymerization through hydrophobic interactions

choices.r: Disulfide bonds form between cysteine residues; valine does not contain a thiol group and cannot form or disrupt disulfide bonds. Hemoglobin's quaternary structure is maintained by non-covalent interactions, not disulfide bonds.
choices.t: Valine disrupts the disulfide bonds that normally maintain hemoglobin's quaternary structure, causing uncontrolled aggregation

choices.r: HbS can bind oxygen; the problem is that deoxygenated HbS specifically polymerizes. The substitution's effect on polymerization is through the hydrophobic surface interaction, not through oxygen-binding capacity. Oxygenated HbS does not polymerize even with valine at position 6.
choices.t: The loss of glutamic acid's negative charge at position 6 directly prevents HbS from binding oxygen, causing polymerization as an indirect consequence

stem: Which best explains the molecular basis for HbS polymerization under low-oxygen conditions?
stimulus: Sickle cell disease results from a single amino acid substitution in β-globin: glutamic acid (polar, negatively charged at pH 7.4) at position 6 is replaced by valine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). Under low-oxygen conditions, sickle hemoglobin (HbS) polymerizes into rigid fibers that deform red blood cells. Normal hemoglobin (HbA) does not polymerize under the same conditions.
subject: biology

choices.t: Fraction 1, nuclei; fraction 2, mitochondria; fraction 3, lysosomes; fraction 4, rough ER fragments.

choices.t: Fraction 1, nuclei; fraction 2, mitochondria; fraction 3, rough ER fragments; fraction 4, lysosomes.

choices.r: The fraction that makes ATP using oxygen is mitochondria, while the acid hydrolases belong to lysosomes, so these two are swapped.
choices.t: Fraction 1, nuclei; fraction 2, lysosomes; fraction 3, mitochondria; fraction 4, rough ER fragments.

stem: Liver tissue is homogenized and separated by centrifugation into four fractions. Fraction 1 contains 85% of the cell's DNA, in linear chromosomes, and little other activity. Fraction 2 carries out most of the oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis when given pyruvate and also contains 8% of the DNA, as small circular molecules. Fraction 3 contains hydrolytic enzymes with an activity optimum at pH 5. Fraction 4 consists of tiny closed vesicles that have ribosomes on their outer surface and make proteins that enter the vesicle interior. Which assignment is best supported?
subject: biology

choices.r: Incorrect. Ribosomes synthesize proteins from mRNA whether or not vesicles form. The drug blocks the movement of the protein, not its synthesis.
choices.t: Amylase is no longer made at all, because ribosomes on the rough ER cannot make proteins unless vesicles leave the ER.

choices.r: Incorrect. The Golgi complex modifies and packages new products, but it is not where amylase is made. In the process described, amylase is made at the rough ER.
choices.t: Amylase is made by ribosomes in the Golgi complex instead, and it is then secreted normally.

choices.r: Correct. The drug blocks the vesicles that carry material from the rough ER to the Golgi complex, so the enzyme cannot move on to be modified, packaged, and secreted.
choices.t: Amylase is still made on the rough ER, but it builds up there, and little reaches the Golgi complex or is secreted.

choices.r: Incorrect. The Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins for trafficking, and secretion depends on the vesicle route. Blocking the route does not speed secretion up.
choices.t: Amylase is secreted faster than normal, because it no longer has to pass through the Golgi complex first.

stem: Which outcome for amylase in the treated cells is most likely?
stimulus: Pancreatic cells secrete the digestive enzyme amylase. Amylase is made by ribosomes on the rough ER. It is then modified and packaged in the Golgi complex, and transport vesicles carry it to the plasma membrane to be secreted. A researcher treats the cells with a drug that blocks the formation of the transport vesicles that carry material from the rough ER to the Golgi complex.
subject: biology

stem: A migrating bird stores 200 g of fat for its flight. Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram, and carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal per gram. What mass of carbohydrate would hold the same energy?
subject: biology

stem: A student measures catalase activity in potato at 5, 20, 35 and 60°C by placing a potato disc in hydrogen peroxide and counting oxygen bubbles for one minute. Which change would most improve the validity of her conclusion about temperature?
subject: biology

stem: Neurotransmitter N is applied to a muscle fiber and depolarizes the membrane within 5 milliseconds. Which conclusion is best supported?
subject: biology

stem: In the same pathway (E1 makes B from A, E2 makes C from B, E3 makes D from C, and D inhibits E1 allosterically), a cell is growing with a moderate level of D that partly inhibits E1. A drug then completely and irreversibly blocks E2. Which change is most likely over the next few minutes?

choices.t: Uptake increases approximately in proportion to the amount of protein T, which supports transport being carried out by protein T in the membrane.

choices.t: Protein T lowers the permeability of the bilayer to glucose, because uptake without the protein is below 5 units.

stem: A researcher adds increasing amounts of purified protein T to liposomes and measures radioactive D-glucose uptake in 10 minutes.
